_README: Approach variants — WASHINGTON OLYMPIC PENINSULA alpine, 2026-08-19. 27 routes, 45 variants, every one carrying a baseFinding.
`area` on every entry was READ FROM THE LIVE ROW (routes.area_id), not typed from the route name. Four of these ids carry no
peak name at all — wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall and wa_washington_ellinor_traverse_ridge are both filed under MOUNT WASHINGTON
(the Olympic one, wa_mount_washington_olympic, not the Exit-38 crag of the same name), wa_lena_lake_to_mt_stone_traverse is
filed under MOUNT STONE, and wa_olympus_traverse under MOUNT OLYMPUS. A name-shaped id is not evidence of which peak you are on.
Scope was the 20 peaks named in the request. Three of those are not in the catalog under an Olympic parent and were not touched:
SAWTOOTH RIDGE (the only `Sawtooth` area in WA is wa_sawtooth_chelan, Central-East Cascades, a different range), LOST PEAK (the
only `Lost Peak` is wa_lost_peak_pasayten, Okanogan), and INNER CONSTANCE / MOUNT CONSTANCE / THE BROTHERS etc. are present and
were covered. wa_andersons_thumb was included as a sub-feature area of the Anderson massif. 37 routes exist in those areas;
30 had an EMPTY approach_variants, 27 are written here and 3 were deliberately skipped — see _SKIPPED.
Contamination rejected during research, recorded so it is not re-introduced:
- 'Mount Cameron' — the first search result for a Cameron west-ridge route is 14ers.com, which is COLORADO's 14,238 ft Mount
Cameron on the Lincoln group. Nothing from that page was used. Only the Olympic peak (7,190 ft, 47.8253 N 123.3284 W,
Jefferson County, triple-summited, class 2) is described here.
- 'Mount Christie' — there is a Mount Christie in ALBERTA and a Christie Mountain ski area; both surfaced in the same search.
Only Olympic National Park's 6,177-6,182 ft Christie above Martins Park and Low Divide was used.
- 'Mount Washington' — WA has at least four: the Olympic peak above Lake Cushman (this one), the Exit-38 crag area
(wa_mt_washington_2), the university campus area, and Oregon's Cascade Mount Washington. Only Big Creek / FR-2419 sources
describing a 6,255 ft Olympic summit were used.
- 'Lake Constance' — there is a Lake Constance in New Zealand and the European Bodensee; both appeared in the coordinate
search. Only the Olympic lake at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon was used. See _DEFECTS: this catalog holds two disagreeing
copies of its coordinate.
- 'Deception' — WA has Deception Pass (Whidbey), Deception Crags and Deception Wall (Exit 38), Deception Falls (Stevens) and
Mount Deception (Olympic). Only the Olympic peak's basin names were used, and only where a source named Royal Basin or the
Dungeness.
- 'Mount Stone' — the name-matched area list also returned Tumblestone, Cobblestone Wall, Blackstone, Tombstone and Gem Stone,
none of them this peak. Only Hamma Hamma / Putvin / Lake of the Angels sources were used.
TWO KNOWN FINDINGS ARE HONOURED RATHER THAN RE-LITIGATED, and both mean the route's NAME points the wrong way:
- wa_mount_christie_west is titled 'West Slopes (Standard)' and every published line on the peak climbs the NORTH side —
the north couloir out of Martins Park to a 5,600 ft north-ridge saddle, across the Christie Glacier to the east col, then
the southeast summit ridge. The variants below describe that line. Do not follow the name west.
- wa_mount_cameron_standard is titled 'Standard Route (Southeast Slopes)' and Cameron Pass lies WEST of the summit; the
climb is a west-ridge walk gained at the pass. The variants below describe that line. Anyone reading 'southeast slopes'
off the row title and descending east off the pass is walking into the Dosewallips headwaters.
No time, distance or gain figure is averaged. Where two sources disagreed, the field is omitted. Most entries carry none —
Olympic mileages are quoted from three different starting points (highway, road washout, actual trailhead) far more often
than they are quoted consistently.

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail to Glacier Meadows, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. Earlier and the trail above Elk Lake is steep snow; later and the moat at the base of the summit rock opens and the ramps go from snow-covered to loose
approach_variants.notes:
From the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center (about 578 ft) the Hoh River Trail runs east up the valley for roughly 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows at about 4,300 ft, past Five Mile Island, the Olympus Guard Station and High Hoh Bridge near mile 9, Lewis Meadow near mile 11 (the usual overnight if you split the walk in), and Elk Lake near mile 15. A washed-out cliffside stretch around mile 16 is crossed on a fixed ladder; rungs have been reported missing in recent seasons, so look at it before you commit weight. Water is frequent the whole way.

From Glacier Meadows a way path climbs about 0.8 mile to the crest of the Blue Glacier's lateral moraine and follows it roughly 0.2 mile before dropping onto the ice. That drop is loose and rockfall-prone; some parties fix a short line. Rope up on the ice. Cross the flat lower glacier and climb moderate snow, threading the rock islands to the right of the main icefall before swinging back left below the massif, to the crest of Snow Dome at about 6,600-6,800 ft. Snow Dome is the standard high camp, a thousand feet below the summit.

From Snow Dome the standard line goes up to and over Crystal Pass, then traverses just south of and below Five Fingers Ridge and over a false summit to the summit pyramid. A large crevasse near Crystal Pass is usually bridged through midsummer.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A FLAT TOP AT THE FOOT OF AN 80 FT TOWER, AND IT WORKS IN CLOUD BECAUSE IT IS UNDERFOOT, NOT ON THE HORIZON. Off the false summit you drop into a sharp saddle, then climb a short steep snow slope with a clean runout. That slope ENDS FLAT. The moment the ground stops rising and you are standing on a small flat platform of snow with an 80 ft rock tower directly above you, you are at the base of the summit block, on its NORTHEAST side. There is nothing else on this mountain that is a flat snow top under an 80 ft tower.

SECOND TEST, and it is the one that separates this finish from the two other rows on this same block: from that platform the East Face Ramps line goes RIGHT, around the corner onto the east face, and climbs a series of ramps angling up and across it before joining the last Class 4 / 5.4 step. If you are climbing straight up the face directly above the platform you are on the North Face Direct, and if you have walked round to the far side you are on the Northwest Edge. All three finish on the same 80 ft tower and all three start from this platform; the only thing that tells them apart is which way you turn.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: if you are still gaining height on snow with no rock tower over you, you are on the five-fingered false summit east of the true one and have not yet dropped into the saddle. If you can see the Blue Glacier below you on your right the whole way, you are still on the traverse and have not reached Crystal Pass.

HONEST LIMIT: the ramps themselves are loose and the correct one is chosen by eye. A fog test can get you to the foot of the block; it cannot pick the ramp for you.
hazards: Crevasses on the Blue Glacier and a large one near Crystal Pass, usually snow-bridged and not always
Rockfall on the moraine descent onto the ice, and a fixed-ladder washout around mile 16 of the trail
Loose rock on the east-face ramps and rockfall from parties above on them
A developing moat at the base of the summit rock in warm or late-season conditions, forcing a committing step onto rock
Whiteout on Snow Dome — the crevassed plateau is where the 1993 fatal unroped fall happened
A 17-mile walk out with no cell coverage

approach_variants.name: From the Bailey Range: Queets Basin, Blizzard Pass and the Humes Glacier
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Bailey Range crest is walkable and the Humes is not avalanching
approach_variants.notes:
This is the approach of parties already on the Bailey Range Traverse rather than a way anyone drives to. It comes at Olympus from the SOUTH instead of the north: from the High Divide out of Sol Duc, along the Bailey crest through Cat Basin, Ferry Basin and Stephen Peak, then down into Queets Basin, and up over Blizzard Pass onto the Humes Glacier. From the Humes the summit massif is gained from the south side and the summit block is reached from the opposite direction to the Snow Dome line.

It is longer by days and it exists in the record because traverse parties use it, not because it is easier. A party carrying glacier gear can also run it the other way and exit down the Blue Glacier to the Hoh, which is how most traverses finish.

Nothing about the approach shortens the climb: the last five hundred feet, the false summit, the saddle and the summit block are the same ground the Hoh parties cross.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE SAME FLAT SNOW TOP UNDER THE 80 FT TOWER — the block does not care which side of the mountain you walked in from. What changes coming from the south is which way you meet the false summit: from the Humes side you are working up toward the summit ridge from below rather than dropping onto it from Crystal Pass, so the sharp saddle between the false summit and the true one is reached from the opposite end.

The test that you have not overshot on this side is Five Fingers Ridge. The standard line runs just SOUTH of and BELOW it. If Five Fingers Ridge is below you rather than above you, you are on the crest itself and too high; drop back under it and keep the ridge on your uphill side until the false summit is passed and the saddle opens.

HONEST LIMIT: this approach is thinly documented as an approach — it is described in traverse accounts, which are about the traverse. Treat the Hoh variant as the one with detail and this one as the one that gets a traverse party to the same platform.
hazards: Multi-day committing wilderness travel with no bail options once on the Bailey crest
Crevasses and icefall on the Humes Glacier
Blizzard Pass holds steep snow and is named for what happens there
Route-finding on the Bailey crest in cloud, where the ridge is the only handrail
No resupply and no reliable rescue access; NPS has reported multiple helicopter rescues per season among permitted Bailey parties

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome to the base of the summit block
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug; early or late season this face can carry ice, which changes it from a 5.4 pitch into something else
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the standard approach for every route on this peak: Hoh River Trail from the Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center about 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows at roughly 4,300 ft, the moraine way path and the drop onto the Blue Glacier, roped glacier travel across the flat lower ice and up through the rock islands right of the icefall to Snow Dome at about 6,600-6,800 ft, then Crystal Pass, the traverse below Five Fingers Ridge, the false summit, and the sharp saddle beneath the true summit pyramid.

The only thing this row changes is what you do once you are standing at the foot of the tower.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SHARED ARRIVAL TEST IS THE FLAT SNOW TOP AT THE FOOT OF THE 80 FT TOWER, on its northeast side, where the steep snow slope out of the saddle stops rising.

THE TEST THAT YOU ARE ON THIS FINISH AND NOT ONE OF THE OTHER TWO IS ROPE, NOT ROCK, AND IT IS THE BEST FOG MARKER ON THIS MOUNTAIN. Enough parties end up on this exact line that a semi-permanent rappel station has built up at the TOP of it — a boulder or horn wrapped in slings with a rap ring and a quick link. From the platform, look straight up the face above you. If there is tat hanging down the line you are about to climb, that is the North Face Direct and you are in the right place. If there is no tat above you, you are looking at the east-face ramps (round the corner to the right) or the northwest edge (round to the left), and you have not found this finish.

The fixed gear is not agency-maintained and slings weather fast, so back it up and do not lower onto it unexamined — but as a piece of route-finding evidence in cloud it is unambiguous, because it is the only fixed anchor on the block and it hangs down THIS face.

SECOND TEST: the pitch is a single rope length of about 165 ft on generally solid rock at 5.4, steeper and more exposed than the ramps. If your first fifty feet is a wandering scramble across ledges rather than a face, you have drifted onto the ramp system.
hazards: Fixed tat at the top of the pitch is old and unmaintained — inspect and back it up
The face is steeper and more exposed than either other summit-block finish, and holds ice early and late in the season
The descent rappel measures close to a full 165 ft, which eats nearly all of a 60 m rope doubled with nothing to spare
Everything on the approach: Blue Glacier crevasses, the Crystal Pass crevasse, moraine rockfall, whiteout on Snow Dome

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome to the base of the summit block
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug, on the same window as every other line on this block
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard one and is identical to the point where you are standing on snow at the foot of the summit tower: Hoh River Trail about 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows, the moraine and the Blue Glacier, Snow Dome at roughly 6,600-6,800 ft, Crystal Pass, the traverse below Five Fingers Ridge, over the false summit, down into the sharp saddle, and up the short steep snow slope to the platform.

The row's own approach text says as much in one line — same as the Blue Glacier / East Face route until the summit block base, approach time identical. The variants here exist to say what to do with your eyes once you are there.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE SHARED ARRIVAL TEST IS THE FLAT SNOW TOP AT THE FOOT OF THE 80 FT TOWER. You reach it on the tower's NORTHEAST side, which matters, because this finish is on the far side from where you arrive.

THE TEST FOR THIS FINISH IS THAT YOU HAVE TO WALK ROUND THE TOWER TO FIND IT. From the platform, the east-face ramps leave to your right and the north face rises directly above you with its rappel tat hanging down it. The Northwest Edge is neither: it is the arete on the opposite side, and reaching it means traversing round the base of the block anticlockwise until the face you are under is no longer the one with the tat on it and the ground has swung round to the northwest.

SECOND TEST, and it is a feel test rather than a sight test, which is what you want in cloud: the rock on this edge is noticeably MORE SOLID than the east-face ramps. The ramps are loose, gravelly and rockfall-prone; the northwest edge is described consistently as clean rock, steeper and more exposed, with several 5.3-5.4 moves. If the first moves off the snow are on rubble-covered ledges you are on the ramps; if they are on positive holds on an exposed edge you are on this line.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: keep traversing anticlockwise past the northwest edge and the ground under the block drops away steeply on the west side with no reasonable line above it. If you are downclimbing to keep going round, stop and come back.
hazards: Significant exposure on the edge, with more air under you than on either other finish
Traversing the base of the block on snow to reach it, above the drop back into the saddle
A moat at the rock-snow junction late in the season
Everything on the approach: Blue Glacier crevasses, the Crystal Pass crevasse, moraine rockfall, whiteout on Snow Dome

approach_variants.name: Hoh River Trail, Blue Glacier and Snow Dome — the traverse begins on the West Peak
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Aug. The Middle Peak's east-side moat is the thing that decides whether this goes at all, and it runs deep in some seasons
approach_variants.notes:
The approach is the standard Olympus approach and nothing else: Hoh River Trail from the visitor center about 17.4 miles to Glacier Meadows at roughly 4,300 ft, with Lewis Meadow near mile 11 the usual overnight; the moraine way path and the loose drop onto the Blue Glacier; roped glacier travel across the lower ice and up through the rock islands to Snow Dome at about 6,600-6,800 ft; then Crystal Pass, the traverse under Five Fingers Ridge, the false summit and the saddle to the West Peak.

What the traverse adds is everything after that: West Peak (7,980 ft) to Middle Peak (7,929 ft) to East Peak (7,762 ft), all of it off-trail glacier and ridge ground, with crevasse and icefall exposure the whole way and a full rescue kit needed for the entire outing rather than just for the West Peak block. Standard exit is toward Glacier Pass and back down to Glacier Meadows.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS ROUTE'S BASE IS A SUMMIT, WHICH IS THE ONE PIECE OF GOOD NEWS IN IT. The traverse starts on the WEST PEAK, and you know you are on the West Peak because you have just climbed an 80 ft rock tower off a flat snow platform — no other high point on this massif is gained that way. If you have not climbed a rock tower, you are on the five-fingered false summit east of the true one and the traverse has not started.

THE TEST THAT DECIDES WHETHER THE TRAVERSE GOES IS A MOAT, AND IT IS AT THE OTHER END. Between West and Middle Peaks the descent to the saddle is careful downclimbing on non-technical ground, but the Middle Peak's EAST side carries a snow moat that in some seasons is too deep to pass. That is the go / no-go, and it is checked by walking to it rather than by looking at it from the West Peak. Parties that find it impassable have exited via Glacier Pass instead, which carries its own icefall hazard — decide that at the moat, not after committing past it.

SECOND TEST, for the icefall: the traverse line has to work around a heavily crevassed section of the upper Blue Glacier. Stay RIGHT of the icefall on the way across and swing back LEFT below the massif. If you are threading crevasses rather than skirting them, you are in the icefall and should back out to the right.

HONEST LIMIT: route-finding between the three peaks is explicitly described as not straightforward, and there is no marker sequence for it. In poor visibility this is a route to turn round on, not to navigate.
hazards: 14-16+ hours of climbing from Glacier Meadows, so cumulative fatigue is itself a hazard
Sustained crevasse and icefall exposure across the whole traverse, not just on the approach
The Middle Peak east-side moat can be impassable and force a different exit
Route-finding between the peaks is poor in flat light and there is no easy retreat mid-traverse
A conditions-dependent short rappel or careful downclimb off the Middle Peak's loose upper rock in some seasons

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk, West Fork to Anderson Pass and the tarn camp
approach_variants.season: Best spring to early summer, while the snow finger below Flypaper Pass is still continuous. By late summer that finger has thinned and steepened and the bergschrund above it has opened
approach_variants.notes:
From US-101 at Brinnon, drive Dosewallips Road to the washout gate — closed to vehicles since the 2002 flood and still closed. Park there. A mountain bike genuinely saves hours on the road miles. A short bypass trail with a few switchbacks gets round the washout, then the abandoned roadbed resumes for roughly 5.6 miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station at about 1,600 ft.

From the ranger station take the Dosewallips River Trail 1.4 miles to the West Fork junction, then the West Fork Trail upstream past Dose Forks, Big Timber and Diamond Meadows to Honeymoon Meadows at 3,527 ft, roughly 8 trail miles on. Expect at least one calf-to-knee ford of the West Fork depending on snowmelt, and substantial blowdown — maintenance has lagged since the road closed. Beyond Honeymoon Meadows the trail climbs past Camp Siberia to Anderson Pass at 4,464 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to a camp on the snowy saddle above a small tarn at about 5,100 ft (Anderson or Valkyrie Lake). Most parties take 7-9 hours trailhead to camp. Fill up at the tarn; there is nothing above it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS FLYPAPER PASS, AND THE TEST IS WHICH THINGS ARE ON WHICH SIDE OF IT. Flypaper Pass at about 6,500 ft is the notch between MOUNT ANDERSON on the east and ECHO ROCK (7,033 ft) on the west. Standing in the notch, Anderson is on your right and Echo Rock on your left when you are facing north through it. If both walls beside you are the same mountain, you are in a gully on a flank rather than in the pass.

THE APPROACH TEST, done before you can see the notch, is the tarn. From the camp saddle, traverse ABOVE the tarn — often still frozen — and take the single steep snow finger that runs up from the far side of it. There is one finger and it goes to one notch. If you are walking round the tarn at its level rather than above it, you have dropped too low and will meet cliffs.

SECOND TEST, and it is the one that says the pass is in the condition you planned for: the finger's steepest section now runs 40 degrees or more. Glacier recession has steepened it well beyond the older guidebook figure of about 30 degrees over 300 vertical feet, so a party that finds it far steeper than the book has not gone the wrong way — the book is old. If it has melted out to bare scree and ice, that is the season telling you to come back earlier, not a route-finding error.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: over the pass the ground drops onto the Eel Glacier and a bergschrund cuts across below the headwall, forcing an end-around to one side. If you are on glacier and looking for a way past a schrund, you are past the base and onto the climb.
hazards: Crevasses on the upper Eel Glacier, including large ones on its eastern slopes
A bergschrund at the head of the Eel that is hardest to cross late in the season, with a short steep step above it
The Flypaper Pass snow finger at 40-45 degrees, firm or icy, steeper than older descriptions state
Glide avalanches and cornice-triggered slides off the cliffs above the glacier terminus
Loose, crumbly meta-sedimentary rock on the final summit scramble
Unbridged fords and heavy blowdown on the West Fork trail, plus roughly 11 miles of closed road at each end

approach_variants.name: East Fork Quinault and Enchanted Valley to Anderson Pass from the west
approach_variants.season: Same window as the standard side — the pass and the snow finger above it decide the season, not the valley
approach_variants.notes:
Anderson Pass is a divide, and the Quinault side of it is a maintained trail too. From the Graves Creek trailhead at the end of the South Shore Quinault road, the East Fork Quinault Trail runs up the valley through Enchanted Valley to the pass. It is a longer valley walk than the Dosewallips side but it is a TRAIL the whole way, with no closed road at the start and no West Fork fords, which in a wet year is the difference between the two.

At Anderson Pass the two approaches become one: leave the maintained trail and follow the climbers' path up the moraine to the tarn camp at about 5,100 ft, then the snow finger to Flypaper Pass.

Mileages published for the Quinault side vary widely with where the count starts and with the current state of the road, so none is quoted here.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL TO THE DOSEWALLIPS VARIANT ABOVE, because both arrive at Anderson Pass and everything above the pass is shared: traverse above the tarn, take the one steep snow finger from its far side, and know you are at Flypaper Pass when MOUNT ANDERSON is on one side of the notch and ECHO ROCK on the other.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is at the pass itself, because you arrive there from the opposite direction. Anderson Pass is a signed trail junction — the West Fork Dosewallips and East Fork Quinault trails meet there, with the Anderson Pass shelter (Camp Siberia) just below on the Dosewallips side at roughly 4,180 ft. The climbers' path leaves NORTH off the pass and up the moraine. If you have walked over the pass and begun descending the other valley, you have missed the turn; it is a boot path, not a signed one.
hazards: Everything above the pass is the same: the 40-45 degree snow finger, the Eel Glacier crevasses and bergschrund, and loose summit rock
A long valley walk with river crossings and blowdown of its own
Arriving at the pass from the west means the shelter and the climbers' path are both below and behind you as you crest it
No cell coverage anywhere on either side

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail and Avalanche Canyon to the North Chute
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Steep hard snow persists longer on the Terrible Traverse than on any other crux on this mountain, which is exactly the point of it
approach_variants.notes:
Road-walk or bike about 5 miles up the washed-out Dosewallips River Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at roughly 1,450 ft. The trail is unmaintained and gains about 3,300-3,400 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft — steep from the first half-mile, exposed roots and rock steps needing hands, no real switchbacks. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours with a pack. Camp at the lake's north end.

From camp, head up into Avalanche Canyon on scree and talus. Firm snow, when it is there, makes this whole section faster and safer than bare scree. This route does NOT take the South Chute: it stays in the canyon and climbs the North Chute higher up. Above the chute the line loses a little height and traverses north on ledges to reach the Terrible Traverse itself at about 7,435 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS THE CAT EARS, AND FOR THIS ROUTE IT IS A NEGATIVE TEST — YOU WANT TO WALK PAST THEM. The Cat Ears are a rock tower standing just LEFT of the notch at the top of the South Chute, and the standard advice on the South Chute is to start climbing east out of the canyon as soon as the Cat Ears come into view. This route bypasses that. Keep going NORTH up Avalanche Canyon on loose talus, past the South Chute entrance, to the mouth of the North Chute further into the canyon. If you have turned east and are climbing toward a notch with a tower just left of it, you are in the South Chute and on the Finger Traverse route instead.

In cloud the Cat Ears are not visible and the discriminator becomes the canyon itself: the South Chute leaves the canyon EARLY and low; the North Chute is reached by staying in the canyon bed and continuing up it. When in doubt, keep walking up the canyon — the error that puts you on the wrong route is turning uphill too soon.

SECOND TEST, at the top of the chute: the Terrible Traverse is not the chute and it is not immediately above it. Above the North Chute the route LOSES a little elevation and traverses NORTH on ledges before it reaches the traverse at about 7,435 ft. If you have topped a chute and gone straight on up, you have not found it. The traverse itself is unmistakable when you arrive: a steep exposed snow crossing directly above a large cliff, or in late season a narrow rock ledge at the base of the icy slope above it. It is called the Terrible Traverse because a slip there does not stop.

WHAT THE SEASON CHANGES: early to mid summer this is hard steep snow wanting an axe, crampons and, for many parties, pickets. Late season it often melts back to that rock ledge, which most parties find more secure. Neither is the wrong condition; they are different climbs.
hazards: The Terrible Traverse crosses steep firm snow directly above a large cliff — an unprotected slip is very likely fatal
Hard, icy neve is common through June and early July; afternoon softening increases slip risk later in the day
Loose rock throughout the North Chute — classic Olympic choss, and rockfall from parties above is a real hazard
Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes, called out specifically for May-June conditions
One of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics, hard on the way down and slick when wet

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow remnant below Crystal Pass is safe or gone
approach_variants.notes:
The long way in, and the one parties choose to avoid the Lake Constance trail. From the same Dosewallips washout, road-walk or bike roughly 5.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail, which climbs south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Published trail mileages differ by several miles depending on where the count starts, so none is quoted. The upper stretch is open meadow and scree with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail and travel cross-country west, dropping into the head of Crystal Basin and climbing to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif. From Crystal Pass descend into UPPER Avalanche Canyon — which is where this variant differs usefully from the lake approach, because it puts you in the canyon ABOVE the lake rather than below it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COMING IN FROM CRYSTAL PASS YOU ENTER AVALANCHE CANYON FROM ABOVE, SO THE CAT EARS TEST RUNS BACKWARDS AND YOU MUST NOT LET IT PULL YOU DOWNHILL. Dropping south into the canyon from Crystal Pass you meet the North Chute's mouth FIRST and the South Chute entrance further down toward the lake. So the discriminator here is: the first chute you can turn up out of the canyon on the Constance side is the one you want. If you are still descending the canyon and have passed a chute on your left, you have gone below it.

THE FIXED LANDMARK THIS SIDE SHARES with the lake approach is the Cat Ears tower and the Thumb formation, both of which sit in the canyon between the two lines. Keep them BELOW you.

ABOVE THE CHUTE THE TEST IS THE SAME AS THE LAKE APPROACH: the route loses a little height and traverses NORTH on ledges to the base of the Terrible Traverse at about 7,435 ft — a steep exposed snow crossing above a large cliff, or a narrow rock ledge in late season.

HONEST LIMIT: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and lingering snow with real route-finding. This variant trades a brutal trail for a navigation problem; in cloud it is the harder of the two.
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and the descent into upper Avalanche Canyon is unmarked
Early-season snow remnant below Crystal Pass may want an axe and, for some parties, a rope
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt — carry it
All the Terrible Traverse hazards above, reached by a longer and more committing line
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Residual snow in the South Chute makes it a far better climb than bare scree does
approach_variants.notes:
From the Dosewallips River Road washout at roughly 700 ft, about 5 miles of road-walk or bike on the closed road, crossing Constance Creek on wooden footbridges near the start, to the unsigned, unmaintained Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,450 ft.

The trail gains roughly 3,300-3,400 ft in 1.8-2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft — one of the steepest approaches in the Olympics. The first half-mile is brutal and eases only slightly into denser forest with exposed roots and rock steps needing hands. Expect scramble-grade tread with no switchbacks and cairn-and-flagging route-finding in places. Budget 2.5-3.5 hours with a full pack. Water at Constance Creek partway and at the lake outlet; treat everything.

The trail skirts the lake's east shore to established campsites at the north end, in a rocky bowl at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon. Most parties camp there rather than going car to car. From camp, head north up scree into the canyon's lower basin, then bend east along a rib.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE TEST IS A TOWER CALLED THE CAT EARS, AND THE PUBLISHED INSTRUCTION IS A TRIGGER RATHER THAN A DESCRIPTION: BEGIN CLIMBING THE SOUTH CHUTE AS SOON AS THE CAT EARS ARE VISIBLE. Follow Avalanche Canyon north from the lake — roughly 0.6 mile — and watch east. The Cat Ears is the tower standing just LEFT of the notch you are aiming for at the top of the chute. The moment it comes into view, turn east and start up. Starting later means more scree; starting earlier puts you on the wrong ground.

IN CLOUD, WHEN THE CAT EARS CANNOT BE SEEN, THE FALLBACK IS THE CHUTE'S OWN SHAPE. The South Chute is a long gully that NARROWS as it climbs, gaining about 1,900 ft from the lake to roughly 6,600 ft at the notch in the south ridge. It is the first substantial gully leaving the canyon eastward above the lake. If the gully you are in is widening rather than narrowing, or if you are still walking north up the canyon bed after well over half a mile, you have passed it and are heading for the North Chute and the Terrible Traverse instead.

SECOND TEST, and it is what confirms you were right about the chute: above the notch you cross a saddle, DROP about 150 ft, and work up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge. A route that only ever goes up is not this one — the deliberate loss of height above the first notch is part of the line. From there the route threads gaps and ledges marked in places by faded WHITE PAINT DOTS. Painted dots are man-made, they do not move, and they are visible at arm's length in fog; if you are seeing them you are on the line.

THE FINGER TRAVERSE ITSELF IS A TACTILE TEST, WHICH IS THE BEST KIND HERE: a downsloping ledge above a large cliff with a HORIZONTAL CRACK running along its top edge, which you jam your fingers into for balance because the footholds are thin. A rusty decades-old set of fixed pitons sits along it. If there is no continuous crack at hand height above the ledge you are standing on, that is not the Finger Traverse.
hazards: The Finger Traverse is a highly exposed, downsloping narrow ledge; footholds are marginal even with the crack in hand
Reversing it on descent goes round a blind corner and most parties find that harder than the way up
1,900 ft of loose scree in the South Chute, which sluffs rock onto parties below
The fixed pitons on the traverse are decades old — do not trust them without inspection
One of the steepest approach trails in the Olympics; the descent takes many parties nearly as long as the climb

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The long alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail entirely. From the Dosewallips washout, road-walk or bike roughly 5.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end. Take the Constance Pass Trail up through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft, then leave the trail and go cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and up to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif.

From Crystal Pass descend south into Avalanche Canyon on an intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, staying toward the north side of the canyon, and continue DOWN the canyon toward the lake until the South Chute opens on your left (east).

This is considerably longer than the lake approach and it exists because the lake trail is brutally steep, unmaintained and blowdown-choked. Most parties on it are on a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
ENTERING THE CANYON FROM CRYSTAL PASS PUTS THE CAT EARS TEST THE OTHER WAY UP: you must descend PAST the North Chute before the South Chute opens. The Cat Ears tower and the formation trip reports call the Thumb both sit in this stretch of canyon, and on this side you pass them going down rather than meeting them going up.

THE RELIABLE TEST ON THIS SIDE IS THE CHUTE'S TOP, NOT ITS BOTTOM. The South Chute tops out at a notch in the SOUTH ridge at roughly 6,600 ft, with the Cat Ears tower standing just left of that notch. Coming down the canyon from Crystal Pass you can pick your entry by which notch the gully above you leads to: the one with a tower just left of it is the South Chute. The chute that leads straight toward the Terrible Traverse without a tower beside its notch is the North Chute.

ABOVE THE CHUTE THE TESTS ARE IDENTICAL to the lake approach and they are the good ones: cross the saddle, LOSE about 150 ft, up a second scree gully to a notch in the summit ridge, then gaps and ledges marked with faded WHITE PAINT DOTS, then a downsloping ledge with a continuous horizontal finger crack along its top edge and old fixed pitons in it.

HONEST LIMIT: the track fades near Crystal Pass and the drop into the canyon is unmarked. This variant is longer and navigationally harder; it is chosen for the trail it avoids, not for the ground it crosses.
hazards: Unmarked cross-country travel between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass, on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass beyond transient snowmelt
Every hazard on the Finger Traverse itself, reached at the end of a longer day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance climbers' trail, then up Avalanche Canyon past the South Chute
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow in the chute is an improvement on the scree, but Avalanche Canyon is named for what runs down it in May and June
approach_variants.notes:
Bike or walk the closed Dosewallips Road (FS 2610) about 5 miles to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail, then the steep, unmaintained trail roughly 3,300 ft in under 2.2 miles to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camp at the north end of the lake.

From the lake, head north into Avalanche Canyon. This route is the parallel couloir further into the canyon: where the standard South Chute line turns east and climbs out early, the North Chute keeps you in the canyon bed longer and climbs from higher up it.

It sees less traffic than the South Chute and is commonly used as one half of a loop — up one, down the other — rather than as a route in its own right. It rejoins the standard line at or just below the Terrible Traverse, and finishes over the summit block and the North Chimney.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE WHOLE ROUTE-FINDING PROBLEM ON THIS ROW IS TELLING THIS CHUTE FROM THE OTHER ONE, AND THE TEST IS: KEEP WALKING UP THE CANYON PAST THE FIRST CHUTE. The published instruction for the South Chute is to start climbing east as soon as the CAT EARS tower is visible, and trip reports describing this line say plainly that you bypass the South Chute entrance and continue up loose talus to the MOUTH OF THE NORTH CHUTE further into Avalanche Canyon. So the discriminator is temporal, not visual: the first opportunity to leave the canyon eastward is the wrong one.

IN CLOUD, where the Cat Ears cannot be seen at all, this is still workable because the test is about the canyon floor under your feet rather than about a skyline. From the lake, follow the canyon NORTH. Do not turn uphill at the first gully. Keep going on the talus until the canyon delivers you to a second, more northerly couloir, and take that.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS ABOVE THE CHUTE, and it is what proves you took the right one: the North Chute leads toward the Terrible Traverse, the steep exposed snow crossing above a large cliff at roughly 7,435 ft. The South Chute leads to a notch at about 6,600 ft with the Cat Ears tower just left of it and then, after a saddle and a 150 ft descent and a second gully, to the Finger Traverse — a downsloping ledge with a horizontal finger crack and old pitons. If you top out and find a finger crack, you took the South Chute; if you top out and find a snow traverse over a cliff, you took this one.

HONEST LIMIT: this chute is documented mostly as a variation inside other parties' loops. It is long, loose and less travelled, and there is no marker sequence inside the gully itself.
hazards: Avalanche hazard in Avalanche Canyon and its chutes is called out explicitly for May-June conditions
A long, loose gully with rockfall onto anyone below
It commits you to the Terrible Traverse rather than the Finger Traverse — the harder and more exposed of the two crossings
Less traffic means less boot track and fewer people to ask

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road and Constance Pass, over Crystal Pass into upper Avalanche Canyon
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The alternative that avoids the Lake Constance trail. Road-walk or bike roughly 5.5 miles from the washout past the Lake Constance turn-off to the road end at the old campground and ranger station, then the Constance Pass Trail south and southwest to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. Leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin, and climb to Crystal Pass on the Constance-Warrior massif.

From Crystal Pass drop south into UPPER Avalanche Canyon. This is the variant that suits this route best of the three Constance rows, because the North Chute is the higher of the two chutes and coming in from Crystal Pass you meet it without walking the whole canyon up from the lake.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THIS IS THE ONE APPROACH WHERE THE NORTH CHUTE IS THE EASY ONE TO FIND, BECAUSE YOU ARRIVE ABOVE IT. Dropping into Avalanche Canyon from Crystal Pass on the intermittent climbers' path, the FIRST couloir that offers a line up onto the Constance side is the North Chute. Take it. If you keep descending the canyon you will next pass the Cat Ears and the Thumb and eventually reach the South Chute entrance and then the lake — every one of which means you have gone below the route.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS THE SAME AS ON THE LAKE APPROACH: this chute delivers you toward the TERRIBLE TRAVERSE, a steep exposed snow crossing directly above a large cliff at roughly 7,435 ft, reached after the line loses a little height and traverses north on ledges. If you top out on a notch with a tower just to its left and then find a saddle, a 150 ft drop and a ledge with a horizontal finger crack, you have found the South Chute and the Finger Traverse instead.

HONEST LIMIT: the climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass, so this variant's own approach is the navigationally hard part, not the chute.
hazards: Unmarked cross-country between Constance Pass and Crystal Pass on talus, scree and lingering snow
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Avalanche and rockfall in the canyon and the chute
Commits to the Terrible Traverse at the end of a long approach day
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end

approach_variants.name: Lake Constance and Avalanche Canyon to the South Gully
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and snow-dependent in a way most Olympic scrambles are not — this line wants snow still bridging the moats in the defile, so early to mid season is better than late
approach_variants.notes:
The shorter of the two ways in, at roughly 8 miles one-way. Bike or walk about 5 miles of closed Dosewallips Road to the unsigned Lake Constance climbers' trail at about 1,425 ft, then the steep unmaintained boot path up the narrow Constance Creek canyon. At roughly 3,100 ft the tread briefly levels on the valley floor beside the creek at a flat bench with an established fire ring and running water — a common rest stop. From there the last 1,700 ft to Lake Constance at 4,800 ft. Camping at the lake is quota-limited May 1 to September 30.

From the lake head north into Avalanche Canyon, barren and rocky in stark contrast to the rainforest below, on faint intermittent climbers' track and snow patches, and continue up-canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THIS CLIMB IS A FORK, AND THE FORK IS MARKED BY A ROCK FORMATION CALLED THE THUMB. Head up Avalanche Canyon to the broad couloir below the Thumb. That is where the South Chute (which belongs to MOUNT Constance) and the South Gully (which belongs to INNER Constance, this route) diverge. Two summits sit above one canyon and the Thumb is the thing that tells the two lines apart.

THE FOG TEST THAT DOES NOT NEED THE THUMB, AND IT IS THE BETTER ONE, IS THE SHAPE OF THE GULLY YOU END UP IN. From the broad couloir, veer RIGHT into a steeper secondary couloir, which narrows into a snow-filled DEFILE. That defile constricts to roughly a two-foot gap with moats five to ten feet deep opening on either side of the snow by mid-to-late season. Nothing else in this canyon does that. If your gully stays broad and open all the way up, you are in the Mount Constance South Chute and climbing the wrong peak.

SECOND TEST, higher: above the defile the snow finger goes discontinuous and you stem repeatedly between snow and rock to get round the moats, with short up- and downclimbs on rock where the snow runs out. A steep finger tops out at a notch on the East Ridge near 7,200 ft, gained by a short Class 3-4 rock step. If you are still on continuous snow with no stemming, you have not reached the defile yet.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE, AND IT IS THE RECORDED WAY THIS ROUTE GOES WRONG: from the East Ridge the line pulls naturally toward the SOUTHWEST summit, which has no easy connection across to the true NORTHEAST high point. Follow the East Ridge crest on Class 2-3 pillow basalt to the northeast top; if the ridge you are on is running away southwest, you are heading for the wrong summit.

SAFETY NOTE THAT IS PART OF THE ROUTE-FINDING: snow blocks calve out of the defile constriction as the day warms — a refrigerator-sized block struck a climber there. Move through it quickly and probe the bridges over the moats before weighting them.
hazards: Deep moats on both sides of the snow finger in the South Gully defile, needing repeated stemming to bypass
Collapsing or sliding snow blocks in the constriction as the day warms — a documented injury
Notoriously loose, rotten Olympic pillow basalt with rockfall on warm days
Easy to be drawn onto the southwest summit, which has no easy access to the true northeast high point
Steep snowfields and a small glacier high on the route early season
The Lake Constance trail is one of the steepest and least maintained in the range

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road to Constance Pass, then Crystal Basin and Crystal Pass
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the snow below Crystal Pass is safe
approach_variants.notes:
About 16 miles one-way and worth it to some parties precisely because it avoids the Lake Constance trail's brutally steep, unmaintained, blowdown-choked lower section. From the Dosewallips washout at roughly 600 ft, bike or walk the closed roadbed — working round the washout on a riverside bypass — roughly 5.5 miles past the Lake Constance turn-off to the old Dosewallips Campground and decommissioned ranger station at the true road end, about 6.5 miles and 1,900 ft of cumulative gain from the gate.

Pick up the Constance Pass Trail and climb south and southwest through forest into subalpine parkland to Constance Pass at about 5,850 ft. The upper stretch is steep open meadow and scree, with the last reliable water at creek crossings below treeline.

From Constance Pass leave the trail, travel cross-country west into the head of Crystal Basin and climb to Crystal Pass, the windswept notch on the Constance-Warrior massif that divides the Dosewallips side from Avalanche Canyon. Expect a two or three day trip with a camp near Constance Pass or in upper Avalanche Canyon.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM CRYSTAL PASS THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS DIRECTLY BELOW YOU RATHER THAN ABOVE YOU, WHICH IS THE ONE REAL ADVANTAGE OF THIS SIDE. Descend south into upper Avalanche Canyon on the intermittent climbers' path through scree and talus, keeping to the RIGHT (north) side of the canyon, past the Thumb, and then contour and climb toward Inner Constance's northeast side.

THE TEST IS STILL THE THUMB AND THE DEFILE, and it still works from above: the fork you want is the one where the South Gully leaves the broad couloir and veers into a steeper secondary couloir that NARROWS to a two-foot gap with deep moats. Coming from Crystal Pass you can also take the northeast side directly — a short step just above the pass leads into a rising traverse along the RIGHT side of the north ridge crest, broken blocky Class 2-3 with occasional Class 4 and low fifth where the crest steepens.

THE FOG TEST FOR THAT NORTHEAST LINE IS WHICH SIDE OF THE CREST YOU ARE ON. Stay on the crest's RIGHT-hand side as you climb. If you have crossed over and are traversing on the other flank, you are off the line, and the rock over there is worse.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: the same trap as the other variant — the mountain pulls toward the SOUTHWEST summit, which does not connect easily to the true northeast high point. Keep working toward the NORTHEAST top.

HONEST LIMIT: the informal climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass and this stretch is talus, scree and early-season snow with real route-finding demands. A rope and axe may be prudent on the snow remnant below the pass early in the year.
hazards: The climbers' track fades near Crystal Pass; unmarked talus, scree and snow between there and Constance Pass
Notoriously rotten pillow basalt with constant rockfall on warm days
A steep, committing chimney and roof section high on the peak that trip reports call the cave of despair
Being drawn onto the southwest summit
No water above Constance Pass except transient snowmelt
Roughly 6.5 miles of closed road at each end

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake, then the Home Creek basin to the boulder camp
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
From US 101 near Sequim Bay State Park turn onto Louella Road, go about a mile to Palo Alto Road and turn left for roughly 1.1 miles to the forest boundary, where Palo Alto becomes Forest Service Road 28. Turn right on FS 2880, pass Dungeness Forks Campground, then stay left on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead just across the Dungeness River bridge. Large parking area, vault toilet, no potable water, Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass required.

Hike Upper Dungeness Trail #833 up the river — easy, shaded, river-grade — to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Camp / Boulder Shelter at roughly 6.1-6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. Continue on the Constance Pass trail as it climbs out of the timber into rocky flowery terrain beneath Warrior Peak and Inner Constance, crossing into Olympic National Park, and drop to Home Lake at about 9.3 miles and roughly 5,308-5,330 ft, some 500 ft below Constance Pass.

From the lake, work up the Home Creek basin south-southwest toward the peak. Camp at the LARGE BOULDERS directly northwest of the summit, just south of Home Creek. That boulder camp is the documented basecamp for this route and it is where the first-ascent party camped.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE STARTS AT THE TOP OF A SCREE FIELD WHERE AN OBVIOUS RAMP BEGINS, AND THE THING THAT IDENTIFIES THE RAMP IS THE BIGGEST CORNER ON THE FACE. From the boulder camp, climb the scree field to the base of the wall and pick up the obvious ramp. Follow it round CLIMBER'S RIGHT of the PROMINENT DIHEDRAL — the one large, unmistakable corner in that section of face — to a steep Class 3/4 gully. If the ramp you are on is taking you LEFT of the big corner, you are on the wrong side of it.

THE SECOND TEST IS AT THE TOP OF PITCH ONE AND IT IS A COLOUR YOU CAN READ AT ARM'S LENGTH: after the first pitch this route turns CLIMBER'S LEFT onto an obvious ledge running along a GREEN-LICHEN-COVERED FACE. Green lichen on rock is visible in cloud in a way a skyline feature is not. If your first pitch does not end at a ledge beneath a lichen-green face, you are not on the Northwest Buttress — and specifically, if you have carried straight on up a crack system instead of stepping left, you are on Sean's Route / Second Wind, which shares this start and diverges exactly here.

WHAT THE ROW'S OWN TEXT ALREADY TELLS YOU, AND IT IS THE HONEST LIMIT: the face is in full view from the boulder camp and from below, and that is described as the only reliable chance you get to pick out the ramp and the green-lichen ledge. Look at it, photograph it and fix the line in your head from camp. This is a route to identify in the evening and climb in the morning; there is no marker sequence that will find it for you if you walk up into the wall in cloud having never seen it.
hazards: Rock quality described by climbers who have scouted it as among the worst in the Olympic Mountains, and as bad as anything in the range near the summit ridge
No fixed gear anywhere on the route — every rappel station on descent has to be built and left
Sparse protection with long runouts
The guidebook description for this line is thin and climbers who know it advise ground-truthing it in person
A 9+ mile approach with meaningful re-ascent over Constance Pass on the way out

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and the boulder camp — the same start as the Northwest Buttress
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the Northwest Buttress: Upper Dungeness Trailhead at the end of FS 2870, Trail #833 to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Camp at roughly 6.1-6.4 miles, then the Constance Pass trail over into Olympic National Park and down to Home Lake at about 9.3 miles. Basecamp is the large boulders directly northwest of the summit, just south of Home Creek. Published approach distance is usually given as about 8.5 miles from the trailhead to basecamp; the northwest face comes into view from below the lake.

This route and the Northwest Buttress share their approach, their camp, their scree field and their first pitch. They are one climb until the top of that pitch. The first-ascent party's round trip from camp — climb plus the descent into Avalanche Canyon and back round to the Home Lake cirque — ran about 12.5 hours.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS SHARED WITH THE NORTHWEST BUTTRESS AND SO IS THE TEST FOR IT: from the boulder camp, up the scree field to the OBVIOUS RAMP, and follow it round CLIMBER'S RIGHT of the PROMINENT DIHEDRAL to a steep Class 3/4 gully. Right of the big corner, not left.

THE TEST THAT SEPARATES THIS ROUTE FROM THE BUTTRESS COMES AT THE TOP OF PITCH ONE, AND IT IS A DECISION RATHER THAN A LANDMARK — WHICH IS WHY IT IS WORTH KNOWING BEFORE YOU LEAVE THE GROUND. At that point the Northwest Buttress steps CLIMBER'S LEFT onto an obvious ledge along a green-lichen-covered face. Sean's Route does NOT. It stays with the crack system and follows it straight on up rotten loose rock for roughly three pitches in total.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS TACTILE, OVERHEAD AND UNMISTAKABLE IN ANY VISIBILITY: about three pitches up, the crack system ends at a CAVE BENEATH AN OVERHANGING ROOF. You cannot mistake being under a roof. That cave is the route's crux and its identity — you build an anchor in it and make a committing move out by underclinging the roof and traversing right about 10 to 15 feet onto the ramp leading to the slab above. If you have climbed three pitches and there is no roof over you, you are on the Buttress or on neither.

HONEST LIMIT: this is a shared base with a pitch-one divergence rather than a route with a base of its own, and it is recorded that way rather than dressed up. Above the roof it is a few pitches of Class 4 to low fifth to the southwest false summit, then it rejoins the Northwest Buttress for the last pitch to the true top. Protection averages one usable placement every 20 to 100 feet.
hazards: Sparse, widely spaced protection — roughly one usable placement per 20 to 100 feet — so fall consequences are severe on the crux pitches
Persistent rockfall on typical loose Olympic basalt, and the first three pitches are explicitly rotten
The move out of the cave is exposed and committing, and retreat from it is not simple
No fixed gear; descent stations must be built
The descent is not the ascent line — it drops into Avalanche Canyon on loose sandy ledges and traverses back round to the Home Lake cirque

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake Trail and the Valley of the Silent Men to the climbers' camp, then the North Peak side
approach_variants.season: June is the usual recommendation, with consolidated snow in the Great Basin; conditions vary a lot year to year
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FR-25 (Hamma Hamma Road) at roughly 685-750 ft, take Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft. Past the lake the trail runs up a remote forested canyon known as the Valley of the Silent Men to the climbers' camp roughly 6 miles from the trailhead. Most parties camp at Lena Lake or at the climbers' camp rather than trying it in a day.

From camp this route splits away from the ordinary South Couloir line: cross the creek westward, cross a slide meadow and old burn scar, and climb a wide gully north to about 5,500 ft to gain the North Peak side of the mountain. The traverse is recommended north to south, so the North Peak is the start and the South Brother is the finish.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A STEP IN THE RIDGE CREST AT ABOUT 6,100 FT, AND THE WAY YOU KNOW IT IS THE RIGHT ONE IS THE THING THAT HAPPENS IF YOU GO 100 FT HIGHER. Working up and rightward from camp on scree, heather and lumpy basalt, crossing many small ribs and gullies, you meet the crest. There are two places you can meet it. The higher one, at about 6,200 ft, is a small notch whose FAR SIDE IS A 200-FOOT CLIFF — a party that tops out there has to back off and traverse out on exposed ledges with Class 3-4 slots between them. The one you want is the small STEP in the crest at about 6,100 ft, from which the ground drops steeply but climbably into the snow-filled Great Basin.

SO THE FOG TEST IS: TOP OUT, THEN LOOK DOWN. If the far side goes, you are at the step and on route. If the far side is a cliff, you are a hundred feet too high — do not try to force it, come back down and traverse.

SECOND TEST, once in the Great Basin: from it you climb a moderately steep snow couloir angling toward the North Brother, narrowing to a snow finger that reaches the summit ridge. If your couloir is running away from the north summit rather than toward it, you crossed the basin in the wrong direction.

WHAT THE TRAVERSE ITSELF FEELS LIKE, so nobody mistakes the connecting ridge for a mistake: the crest between the two Brothers is giant boulders forming a jagged run of horns and pinnacles, and traversing it is slow. Slow is correct here. The route is roughly seven roped pitches — fourth class to the notch, steep snow into the Great Basin, moderate snow on the east ridge, a sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side, mixed ground with moat belays, and a final steep couloir to the South Brother.
hazards: The 6,200 ft notch drops onto a 200 ft cliff — a documented dead end that costs time and exposes a party on retreat ledges
Steep snow descent into the Great Basin
Exposed fourth-class scrambling to the notch
A sparsely protected rock traverse on the west side of the ridge
Moat belays on the mixed sections, which move with the season
A long committing day with no easy bail once across the Great Basin

approach_variants.name: North Fork Quinault to Low Divide, then Martins Park and the north couloir
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Firm morning snow in the couloir is what makes this line reasonable; late season it thins to loose rock
approach_variants.notes:
READ THE NAME ON THIS ROW WITH CARE — it says West Slopes and the climb is on the NORTH side. Every published account climbs the north couloir out of Martins Park to a north-ridge saddle, crosses the Christie Glacier to a col east of the summit, and finishes up the southeast ridge.

From the North Fork Quinault Ranger Station at roughly 500 ft, at the end of the North Fork Quinault River Road about 17 miles east of US-101 at Lake Quinault, follow the North Fork Quinault River Trail upstream past Wolf Bar at about 2.5 miles, Halfway House Camp near 5 miles, Elip Creek near 6.5 miles, Trapper Shelter near 8.1 miles (day and emergency use only), a ford of the North Fork at Sixteen Mile Camp near 13.2 miles that can run thigh-deep in high water, and Low Divide near 15.3-16.7 miles, which sits on the actual Quinault-Elwha drainage divide.

From Low Divide take the rough fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin and camp there.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM LOWER MARTINS PARK THERE IS ONE BROAD SNOW-AND-ROCK COULOIR AND IT RUNS SOUTH TOWARD THE PEAK. That is the whole arrival test and it is why parties consistently report finding it easily: you walk out of the lower meadows and over to the base of the snowfield. You are at the base when the meadow ends and continuous snow begins, with the couloir running away from you SOUTH — not west. If the drainage you are looking up runs any other direction, it is not this one.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS A NUMBER AND A DURATION: the couloir gains about 2,100 ft and tops out at a SADDLE ON THE NORTH RIDGE near 5,600 ft, and parties consistently report about three and a half hours for it. If you have climbed far more than 2,100 ft without reaching a saddle, you are in the wrong gully.

SECOND TEST, past the saddle, and it is the one that catches the real trap on this peak: from the saddle you DROP down loose gravelly slopes to the lower edge of the CHRISTIE GLACIER. A route that only ever climbs is not this one. Rope up — reports describe few or no open crevasses but the angle is enough that parties treat it as glacier ground anyway. At the top of the glacier a MOAT forms where ice meets rock; in a good year it is a single easy step across to the high col. Check it before committing, because it is the thing that changes year to year.

WHAT WAITS AT THE COL, so it is not a surprise: the barrier above it is a chossy eroded cliff band, very steep to locally overhanging, and it is the crux of the peak, not a formality. It has changed between recent seasons — one party found the expected weakness gone and had to force a line to the right across an extremely loose, essentially unprotectable ledge on a tight rope. Expect dense krummholz above it before the rock improves and the Class 2-3 southeast ridge leads to the summit.
hazards: A loose, chossy, poorly protected Class 4 step above the high col that has changed between seasons — treat published descriptions of it as provisional
Glacier travel on the Christie Glacier with a moat at its top whose width varies year to year and by time of day
Steep snow in the entry couloir with runout risk, and refreezing snow in it on a late return
Dense subalpine krummholz above the col
A thigh-deep ford of the North Fork Quinault at Sixteen Mile Camp in high water
Extreme remoteness — an injury near the summit means a multi-day self-extraction or a helicopter

approach_variants.name: Elwha side to Low Divide, from Whiskey Bend
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, on the same window as the Quinault side
approach_variants.notes:
Low Divide is a divide, and the Elwha reaches it from the north just as the Quinault does from the south. Historically this meant the Elwha River Trail from the Whiskey Bend Trailhead. Since the September 2024 Olympic Hot Springs Road washout, Whiskey Bend has been closed to vehicles, which adds an extra 6.2 miles each way on foot or by bike from the Madison Falls parking area simply to reach the trailhead — check current road status before choosing this side, because that closure is what decides whether it is competitive with the Quinault.

From Low Divide the route is identical to the Quinault variant: the fisherman's path into Martins Park and the Martin Lakes basin, camp, and the north couloir.

No mileage is quoted for this side because published figures assume Whiskey Bend is drivable and most currently are not.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL TO THE QUINAULT VARIANT ONCE YOU ARE AT LOW DIVIDE, and that shared test is a good one: from LOWER Martins Park there is ONE broad snow-and-rock couloir and it runs SOUTH toward the peak. Walk to where the meadow ends and the snow begins. Up it about 2,100 ft, roughly three and a half hours, to a saddle on the NORTH ridge near 5,600 ft; then DOWN loose gravel to the Christie Glacier; then the moat at the glacier's top and the high col east of the summit.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is at Low Divide itself, because you arrive from the opposite direction. Low Divide is a trail junction and the site of the historic ranger station, and it is where the climbers' route LEAVES maintained trail for Martins Park. Coming up from the Elwha, that turn is on your right as you crest the divide and it is a rough fisherman's path, not a signed one. If you have started descending toward the Quinault, you have walked past it.
hazards: Road closure at Olympic Hot Springs Road adds 6.2 miles each way and may change season to season
Everything above Low Divide is the same as the Quinault variant: the Class 4 step above the col, the Christie Glacier moat, and the entry couloir
A long Elwha valley walk with river crossings
No cell coverage and multi-day self-rescue exposure

approach_variants.name: Obstruction Point Road, Grand Pass and the Cameron Pass Trail
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by the road: Obstruction Point Road is usually open only early-to-mid July through mid-October
approach_variants.notes:
READ THE NAME ON THIS ROW WITH CARE — it says Southeast Slopes, and Cameron Pass lies WEST of the summit. The climb is a west-ridge walk gained at the pass. A party that reads the title and heads southeast off the pass is walking into the Dosewallips headwaters.

Drive the narrow one-lane gravel Obstruction Point Road — Olympic National Park's highest road, topping out at 6,135 ft — 8 miles east from the Hurricane Ridge Visitor Center to the Obstruction Point trailhead. Hike the Grand Pass Trail roughly 6 miles to Grand Pass at about 6,450 ft; the drop off the far side toward Cameron is steep and slick in wet weather or lingering snow. The trail then crosses several unbridged branches of Cameron Creek in a wet meadow — reliable water, and tread that is easy to lose in fog or high brush — to the Cameron Basin camps at about 6,000 ft near 8.3 miles, and on up to Cameron Pass at roughly 6,450-6,500 ft near 9.3 miles. Bear canister required in the basin; there are no trees to hang food. Steep snow can persist on the pass into late July or August and the climbers' path is frequently buried there.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS CAMERON PASS AND THE TEST IS THE DIRECTION YOU TURN OUT OF IT: THE RIDGE YOU CLIMB RISES TO THE EAST. The pass is west of the summit. From it, leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest EAST and UP. If the ground under you is falling away, or you are contouring around a slope rather than walking a crest, you are not on the route — the correct line is a ridge, and a ridge in cloud is identifiable by the fact that the ground drops on both sides of you.

SECOND TEST, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST HERE: THE RIDGE IS A SEQUENCE OF FALSE SUMMITS. It is mostly Class 1-2 and it crosses many bumps before the true summit. So a high point that arrives sooner and more easily than you expected is a false one. Do not stop on the first thing that stops going up; keep the crest under you and keep going until a short Class 3-4 section leads to the top — that step is the deciding feature of the peak.

THIRD TEST, for the far end: Cameron is a triple summit and the crest continues past the true top toward the Middle Peak, which has spots of Class 3-4, and then to the East Peak. If you have started descending steeply and then re-climbing on harder ground, you have gone past the true summit and are onto the traverse. That is a legitimate outing; it is not this route.

HONEST LIMIT AND A LIVE DISAGREEMENT: this row's own summit waypoint calls the EAST Peak the true 7,190 ft high point, while traverse accounts reach the true summit FIRST from Cameron Pass and then go on to Middle and East. Those cannot both be right. Carry a map, count your summits, and do not treat either the row title or the waypoint name as settled — see _DEFECTS.
hazards: Route-finding on open off-trail slopes above Cameron Basin, and faint brushy tread on the Cameron Pass Trail beyond the basin
Steep lingering snow on Cameron Pass into late July or August, over a buried climbers' path
Loose rock, scree and talus on the summit slopes and along the ridge connecting the three summits
No reliable water above Cameron Basin and minimal to no cell coverage
Obstruction Point Road closes for most of the year and is not a route you can count on before July

approach_variants.name: Deer Park and the Cameron Creek Trail
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and it opens earlier than Obstruction Point in some years because Deer Park Road is a different road on a different aspect
approach_variants.notes:
The other trail-based way into Cameron Basin, and the one worth knowing when Obstruction Point Road is still closed. From Deer Park, the Grand Ridge and Cameron Creek trail system leads into the Cameron Creek drainage and up to Cameron Basin and Cameron Pass from the northeast.

It is longer than the Obstruction Point line and much of the Cameron Creek tread receives little to no maintenance — trip reports describe bushwhacking through dense growth, chest-high berry bushes, and log crossings barricaded by jams. Long sleeves and trousers are recommended by everyone who has written it up.

Once at Cameron Pass the climb is identical to the Obstruction Point variant.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL ONCE YOU ARE AT CAMERON PASS: leave the trail and follow the broad ridge crest EAST and UP, over many false summits, until a short Class 3-4 step leads to the top. The pass is WEST of the summit whatever the row title says.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is in Cameron Basin, because you arrive up the creek rather than over Grand Pass. The Cameron Creek tread crosses several unbridged branches of the creek in wet meadow and is genuinely easy to lose in brush or fog. The handrail is the creek: stay with the drainage and keep climbing it toward the basin at about 6,000 ft. The established camps in the upper basin are the confirmation that you are in the right cirque, and the pass is above them.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: if you crest a pass and the ground beyond drops steeply into a large river valley to the south, you are looking at the Dosewallips headwaters and you have crossed Cameron Pass rather than turning up the ridge at it.
hazards: Long stretches of unmaintained, brushy tread with log jams at creek crossings
Route-finding in wet meadow where the tread disappears
All the summit-ridge hazards of the standard variant, reached after a longer approach
Bear canister required; no reliable water above the basin

approach_variants.name: Dosewallips road walk and the long push up-valley into Cameron Basin
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Recorded because it is what the row's own approach_logistics still points at, and because it is a real historical approach — but it is rarely chosen today and this batch does not recommend it over the two above.

From Brinnon, the Dosewallips River Road has been closed to vehicles at a washout about a mile in since 2002. That forces a long walk or bike up the old roadbed before you even reach the Dosewallips River Trail, and then a multi-day push up-valley into Cameron Basin. It adds many miles over either northern approach.

If you take it, the climb from Cameron Pass is unchanged.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL AT THE PASS: the ridge rises EAST out of Cameron Pass, over many false summits, to a short Class 3-4 step and the true top.

THE TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS IS ABOUT WHICH VALLEY YOU ARE IN, because approaching from the south you come up beneath the peak's southeast face — the aspect the row's title wrongly names — and it does not go. Cameron's southeast side rises over 3,300 ft above the Dosewallips River in about one horizontal mile. If you are standing under that and looking for a line up it, you are on the wrong side of the mountain: the route is the west ridge, gained at the pass, and getting there from this side means continuing up-valley and round into Cameron Basin first.

HONEST LIMIT: this is the approach the on-file trailhead record names and it is not the one the on-file approach prose describes. See _DEFECTS.
hazards: Many extra miles including a long closed-road walk at each end
A multi-day valley approach with fords and blowdown
The southeast face of Cameron is not a route and the approach passes beneath it
All the summit-ridge hazards of the standard variant

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail, Camp Handy and Boulder Shelter to the southeast cirque
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. Snow in the summit couloir into early season is an improvement on the scree that replaces it
approach_variants.notes:
From US-101 near Sequim Bay State Park turn on Louella Road for a mile, then Palo Alto Road for 1.1 miles to the forest boundary, where Palo Alto becomes FS Road 28. Right on FS 2880 past Dungeness Forks Campground, then left on FS 2870 for 8.7 miles to the Upper Dungeness Trailhead. Northwest Forest Pass or interagency pass required at the kiosk.

Trail #833.2 is the shortest and easiest approach. Hike 3.2-3.4 miles and about 600 ft to Camp Handy at roughly 3,100 ft, a riverfront meadow with a cedar-shingle shelter, then take the uphill fork and continue about 3 miles and 1,850 ft to Boulder Camp / Boulder Shelter at 6.3-6.4 miles and roughly 4,890-4,950 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the approach.

From Boulder Shelter hike SOUTH about 2 miles on the Dungeness / Constance Pass trail, crossing several creeks, toward Home Lake.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST TEST IS A CREEK YOU MUST NOT CROSS. Leave the trail BEFORE crossing the major stream that drains the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque. That stream is the last and largest of the several you meet going south from Boulder Shelter. Then climb EAST — steep forest, then steep open meadow, then talus — STAYING NORTH OF THE STREAMBED the whole way. The streambed is the handrail and it stays on your right. If you have crossed it and it is now on your left, you are on the wrong side of the drainage.

THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE CIRQUE AT ABOUT 5,900 FT, and it is unambiguous because it is a closed basin: the ground stops rising in front of you and the headwall closes round. From there, head NORTH to the obvious COULOIR BETWEEN THE TWO PEAKS. Warrior has twin summits and the couloir runs up between them to a saddle at about 7,000 ft. There is one gully in that headwall with a summit on each side of it. If the gully you are in has a summit on only one side, it is not the one.

THE TEST AT THE TOP OF THE COULOIR IS WHICH WAY TO TURN, AND IT IS THE SINGLE MOST USEFUL SENTENCE FOR THIS PEAK IN FOG: AT THE SADDLE, THE HIGHER PEAK IS ON YOUR RIGHT. The southeast summit is the true top; the northwest summit at roughly 7,285 ft is the lower one. Coming up the couloir from the cirque, the true summit is to the RIGHT. Turn left and you will climb the wrong peak on ground just as loose.

SECOND TEST, on the summit block: above the saddle there is 20 to 50 feet of exposed, poor-quality rock rated Class 4 to low fifth on the block's NORTHWEST side, often gained over steep snow or a snow moat, and many parties fix a hand line on it. If your last obstacle before the top is a walk rather than a short difficult rock step, you are on the wrong summit.

WHAT THE SEASON CHANGES: the couloir is steep but straightforward when snow-filled, common early season; melted out it is a brutal scree slog to the same saddle. Both are the route.
hazards: Loose, poor-quality rock on the final headwall above the 7,000 ft saddle — a recurring theme in every account
Rockfall in the couloir between the twin summits, worst with parties above or after freeze-thaw
Glissade and uncontrolled-slide risk descending the snow chute if the runout is not fully visible — one party described nearly going over a cliff band on nearby terrain
Faint use-trail-only route-finding above the trail through forest, meadow and talus
Fast-moving Pacific frontal systems and late-summer afternoon thunderstorms

approach_variants.name: Home Lake basecamp, from either the Dungeness or the Dosewallips side
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Home Lake at about 5,308-5,330 ft, walled in by Mount Constance and Warrior Peak just below Constance Pass, is the standard basecamp for this climb and it is reachable from two directions: north up the Upper Dungeness / Constance Pass trail at roughly 9.3 miles from the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, or south from the Dosewallips road end over Constance Pass. An Olympic National Park wilderness permit is required.

Camping at Home Lake rather than pushing from Boulder Shelter turns this into a comfortable two-day trip and puts you a mile from the cirque. It is also the camp shared with Mount Fricaba, Mount Mystery and Mount Deception parties, so it is well-used ground with an established site.

From the lake, leave the basin and climb EAST into the Warrior / Inner Constance cirque through meadow and talus.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FROM HOME LAKE THE TEST IS THE SAME STREAMBED, WORKED FROM THE OTHER END: leave the lake basin heading EAST into the cirque, STAYING NORTH OF THE STREAM that drains it. The stream is the handrail either way — approaching from Boulder Shelter you must not cross it, and approaching from the lake you must keep it below and to your right as you climb.

THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE SAME CLOSED CIRQUE AT ABOUT 5,900 FT, and then the obvious COULOIR BETWEEN THE TWO PEAKS running north to the saddle at about 7,000 ft — the one gully with a summit on each side of it.

AND THE SAME TURN AT THE TOP: AT THE SADDLE THE HIGHER, TRUE SUMMIT IS ON YOUR RIGHT (southeast). The 20 to 50 ft Class 4 / low fifth step on the block's northwest side is the last obstacle; if there is no step, you are on the northwest summit.

HONEST LIMIT: this variant differs from the one above only in where you sleep and which direction you walk in. It is recorded separately because the row is titled for the Home Lake approach and a reader should not have to reconcile that with an approach description that starts from Boulder Shelter.
hazards: Same as the Boulder Shelter variant: loose summit rock, couloir rockfall, glissade runout, faint route-finding
Home Lake sits below Constance Pass, so an exit north regains meaningful height before the long descent
Wilderness permit required and the site is popular with parties climbing four different peaks
