approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail from Hamma Hamma Road to Lake of the Angels
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Snow lingers in the north-facing basin above the lake well into summer
approach_variants.notes:
From the Putvin Trailhead on Hamma Hamma River Road (FS 25) at about 1,565-1,600 ft — an unmarked roadside pullout, roughly 4.5 miles past the Lena Lake Trailhead — the Putvin Trail is an unmaintained, primitive user trail that climbs steeply and directly from the first steps. Expect root-staircase steps and boot-track tread through forest for the first mile. In recent years a slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles of road, adding a road-walk; check Forest Service status.

About halfway up the trail meets a rock headwall requiring hand-over-hand climbing, with a large tree root as the key handhold and, historically, a fixed handline on the steepest pitch. Above it the trail eases into subalpine forest and heather meadows, passing near Whitehorse Basin and the Pond of the False Prophet, and reaches Lake of the Angels at roughly 4,850-4,920 ft in a cirque below Mount Stone's south face — about 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft of gain. Little to no reliable water on the lower trail; carry enough to reach the lake.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS A NOTCH IN MOUNT STONE'S WEST RIDGE, AND THE TEST FOR IT IS A TURN YOU MAKE BEFORE A GATE. From Lake of the Angels contour and climb toward ST. PETER'S GATE — the obvious notch above the basin. JUST BEFORE THE GATE, TURN SHARPLY LEFT (SOUTH) and traverse along the BASE OF THE CLIFFS to a notch in the west ridge. If you walk through St. Peter's Gate, you have gone too far; the Gate is the marker you turn short of, not the one you pass through.

That works in cloud because the cliff base is a tactile handrail: once you have made the turn, you keep rock on one side of you the whole traverse. Lose contact with the cliff and you have drifted downhill.

SECOND TEST, at the notch: turn RIGHT and climb toward a first sub-summit rock, then up a short LOW CLASS 3 CHIMNEY to its top. A chimney is a shape you can feel with both hands. If the first difficulty above the notch is a face or a slab rather than a chimney you can bridge, you are not on the line.

THIRD TEST, on the summit spire: from the sub-summit cross a brief, somewhat exposed ridge to the base of the true summit spire, then follow a GROOVE on the LEFT side that BENDS RIGHT, where a faint climbers' path leads the last steps to the top. Left then right — a groove that runs straight up is not it.

WHAT THE ROW'S OWN TIMING SAYS: about 2.5 hours up from the Lake of the Angels camp and about 1.5 hours back down. If you have been on the ground above the lake far longer than that without finding the notch, you have most likely missed the turn short of the Gate.

FOG WARNING SPECIFIC TO THIS MOUNTAIN: Mount Stone has more than one summit, and parties have confused the true south summit with the Middle and North summits in cloud. Count your ridges.
hazards: Trail-less, route-finding-dependent terrain above Lake of the Angels
Near-vertical root and rock steps on the lower Putvin Trail, genuinely exposed when wet, and worse descending on tired legs
Loose rock on the headwall and summit block with rockfall onto parties below
An ambiguous Class 3/4 crux near the summit
Fog is common here and multiple parties have lost the route on the upper mountain

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and Upper Lena Lake, the St. Peter's traverse from the east
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the off-trail benches and passes are largely clear
approach_variants.notes:
The other side of the same notch. From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at roughly 600-750 ft, take the well-graded Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage roughly 3.5 more miles to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft, some 6.5 miles and 4,000 ft from the trailhead. Upper Lena Lake is the last maintained-trail camp and the last reliable water before the traverse goes cross-country; wilderness permit and bear canister required.

From Upper Lena Lake, leave the trail and head west on the Scout Lake way-trail across meadows and heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down slightly to Upper Scout Lake, round it into Scout Basin, and up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above the tarns known as Ullin's Bathtubs. From there a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone that ends at a loose moraine, and then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

This is a two- or three-day trip and it is chosen for the country it crosses, not because it is quicker.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COMING FROM THE EAST YOU ARRIVE AT ST. PETER'S GATE ITSELF, WHICH IS THE HIGH POINT OF THE TRAVERSE AT ABOUT 5,950 FT AND AN OBVIOUS ROCKY NOTCH IN MOUNT STONE'S SOUTHEAST RIDGE. That is the arrival test and it is unmistakable in any weather: the ground stops rising, the notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens on the far side.

FROM THE GATE THERE ARE TWO WAYS ONTO THE PEAK AND THEY ARE DIFFERENT CLIMBS. The one this row describes is the west-ridge notch: go THROUGH the Gate and drop toward the Lake of the Angels basin, then work back up and turn the corner onto the cliff-base traverse to the notch in the WEST ridge — the same notch the Putvin parties reach by turning sharply left just short of the Gate. The other is the south-face gully, which starts by descending about 300 ft from the Gate to the base of a basalt cliff; that is the Lena Lake traverse row's line, not this one.

SO THE FOG TEST FOR THIS VARIANT IS WHICH SIDE OF THE GATE YOU END UP ON: this route goes over to the Lake of the Angels side and approaches the west ridge from the south-west, keeping the cliff base at your shoulder.

ABOVE THE NOTCH THE TESTS ARE IDENTICAL to the Putvin variant: turn right, low Class 3 CHIMNEY to a sub-summit, a brief exposed ridge, then a GROOVE on the LEFT that BENDS RIGHT to the true south summit.
hazards: Extensive off-trail way-trail route-finding over multiple passes and basins with faint tread
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate and exposed dirt-and-mud slopes on the final ramp
Fog on the upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route here and ended up in harder terrain
No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass
A very long approach with limited bail options partway through

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail #813 to Lake of the Angels, then the rock rib above the basin
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep. Consolidated snow has been reported from about 4,500 ft up well into summer in the north-facing basin above the lake
approach_variants.notes:
SEE _DEFECTS — this row and wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels appear to be the same climb entered twice. The variants here are written for the ground the row itself describes.

Park at the Putvin Trailhead (FST 813) at about 1,565 ft on Hamma Hamma Road (FR 25). A slide near road mile 10.5 has at times blocked the last 1.2 miles; check Forest Service status. The trail follows the west side of Boulder Creek a few hundred feet, then starts a long unrelenting climbing traverse west, gaining nearly 3,000 ft in under 4 miles without easing.

Around 1.3 miles it crosses an OLD LOGGING ROAD, and the tread is easy to lose there — look for the continuation slightly DOWNHILL. Around 4,200 ft comes the short headwall with an old hand-line or a large exposed tree root as the handhold, the crux of the trail and a common turnaround point when wet. Maintained tread ends in a basin around 3.9 miles at about 4,500 ft, and a rougher way-trail continues up steep rocky ground to Lake of the Angels at about 4,900 ft near 4 miles.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIMB STARTS WHERE THE TRAIL ENDS, AND THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A RIB, NOT A SUMMIT VIEW. From Lake of the Angels the route leaves any trail: climb roughly 800 ft up onto the ROCK RIB above the lake's basin and CROSS TO ITS NORTH SIDE. A rib is a shape underfoot — the ground rises to a spine and falls away on both sides — so it is identifiable in cloud, and the instruction to cross to the far side of it is a check you can perform without seeing anything.

SECOND TEST: from the north side of the rib, Class 2-3 terrain leads up toward a NOTCH ON MOUNT STONE'S WEST RIDGE, BELOW the feature called ST. PETER'S GATE. Below, not through. St. Peter's Gate is the notch in the SOUTHEAST ridge and it belongs to the traverse from Lena Lake; the notch you want is on the WEST ridge and sits lower and to the south of it. If you have walked up to a notch that opens onto an entirely different basin to the east, that is the Gate and you are past your turn.

THIRD TEST, on the summit block: the final 150 to 200 ft is mostly Class 3 but contains one well-documented 15 to 20 ft CLASS 4 STEP up a SHALLOW CRACK, often marked by a CAIRN. A cairn is man-made and does not move. If you have reached the top without meeting a short crack step, you are on a sub-summit — this mountain has three, and parties confuse them in fog.

WHAT THE ROW'S OWN TIMING SAYS: Mountaineers reports for this line log around 5.5 hours up and 4 hours down, roughly 10 hours car to car.

CAUTION FROM A TRIP REPORT, and it is route-finding advice rather than a hazard note: at least one party took a steep mossy waterfall gully as a descent shortcut and found it far worse than reversing the ascent. Reverse the rib; do not improvise a line down the south side.
hazards: Exposed scramble moves near the summit block and a 15-20 ft Class 4 crack step with no fixed anchor
Lingering steep snow in the north-facing basin above the lake into early-mid summer
Route-finding above Lake of the Angels is loose and nontrivial in cloud or fresh snow
The 4,200 ft headwall on the trail is greasy when wet and the hand-line is not maintained
The tread is easy to lose where it crosses the old logging road at about 1.3 miles

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake and the St. Peter's traverse, arriving at the Gate from the east
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The long way to the same mountain, kept here because it is a genuinely different approach rather than a variation of the Putvin walk. Lena Lake Trail #810 about 3 miles to Lena Lake, then the steep primitive tread up the West Fork to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft and 6.5 miles. From there, off-trail west past Lena Tarn and Scout Lake to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down to Upper Scout Lake and round into Scout Basin, over Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft above Ullin's Bathtubs, then a rising traverse to a snow ramp across a steep hillside below Mount Stone, ending on loose moraine, and finally exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft.

Most parties then continue southwest about half a mile into the Lake of the Angels basin, which is where this approach rejoins the Putvin ground, and exit down the Putvin Trail — a different trailhead about 4 road miles from Lena Lake, so plan a shuttle or a stashed bike.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS ST. PETER'S GATE AT ABOUT 5,950 FT: the traverse's high point, an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's SOUTHEAST ridge, reached up a steep snow-and-dirt ramp over loose moraine. Ground stops rising, notch pinches, and the Lake of the Angels basin opens beyond.

THE TEST THAT PUTS YOU ON THIS ROW'S LINE RATHER THAN THE GULLY LINE: from the Gate, continue southwest into the Lake of the Angels basin and pick the route up from there — the rock rib above the lake, crossed to its NORTH side, and Class 2-3 ground to the notch on the WEST ridge below the Gate. The alternative from the Gate is to drop about 300 ft directly to the base of a basalt cliff and take the south-face gully; that is the Lena Lake traverse row, a Class 3-4 gully, and a different climb.

ABOVE THE WEST-RIDGE NOTCH THE TEST IS THE SAME: a short Class 4 step up a shallow crack, often cairned, in the last 150 to 200 ft, on a mountain with three summits.

HONEST LIMIT: coming from the east adds a day and several passes of unmarked way-trail. It is chosen for the country, not for the climb.
hazards: Extensive off-trail route-finding across Scout Pass, Scout Basin and Ullin's Pass on faint tread
Loose glacial moraine and exposed dirt slopes below St. Peter's Gate
Requires a car shuttle or stashed bike between two trailheads about 4 road miles apart
Fog on the upper mountain, where parties have repeatedly lost the route
Unbridged stream crossings on the way-trail sections

approach_variants.name: Lena Lake, Upper Lena Lake and the way-trails to St. Peter's Gate
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once Scout Pass and Ullin's Pass are largely clear; many parties still carry an axe
approach_variants.notes:
From the Lena Lake Trailhead on FS 25 at about 750 ft, the well-maintained Lena Lake Trail #810 runs about 3 miles through second- and old-growth forest along Lena Creek to Lena Lake at about 1,800 ft. Beyond the lake the trail narrows to steep primitive tread up the West Fork Lena Creek drainage, roughly 3.5 more miles and 2,200 ft to Upper Lena Lake at about 4,550 ft — 6.5 miles and about 4,000 ft from the road, the last reliable water and the last maintained-trail camp.

From Upper Lena Lake the traverse goes cross-country: the Scout Lake way-trail west across meadows and huckleberry-heather past Lena Tarn to Scout Pass at about 5,200 ft, down to Upper Scout Lake, contour high round it into Scout Basin, then up to Ullin's Pass at about 5,000 ft overlooking Ullin's Bathtubs. From Ullin's Pass a rising traverse above the small lakes leads to a snow ramp angling across a steep hillside below Mount Stone, ending at a loose grungy moraine, then exposed dirt-and-mud slopes to St. Peter's Gate at about 5,950 ft — roughly 2.2 miles and 2,200 ft above Upper Lena Lake.

No dependable water between Upper Lena Lake and the tarns near Ullin's Pass.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE SUMMIT CLIMB IS 300 FT BELOW ST. PETER'S GATE, AND THE FIRST MOVE IS DOWNHILL — WHICH IS THE WHOLE TEST. Reach the Gate (the traverse's high point at about 5,950 ft, an obvious rocky notch in Mount Stone's southeast ridge). Cache your overnight packs there. Then DESCEND ABOUT 300 FT to the BASE OF A BASALT CLIFF. The climber's path up the south-face gully starts at the foot of that cliff. A route that goes up from the Gate is not this one.

That is a good fog test precisely because it is counter-intuitive: standing in a notch with the summit above you, the instruction is to lose height first and pick the line up from underneath the cliff band.

SECOND TEST, in the gully: it is a vague climber's path up a Class 3-4 gully on Mount Stone's SOUTH face, and it leads into a ROCK BOWL below the summit block. The bowl is the confirmation — an enclosed basin of rock, not a ridge and not open slope. From it the line joins the standard west-ridge route for a final 100 ft or so of Class 2-3 scrambling on SOLID PILLOW BASALT to the true south summit. That last detail is worth trusting: the rock at the top of this peak is noticeably better than anything below it, so if the last hundred feet is still rubble you have not reached the summit ridge.

WHAT GOES WRONG HERE, AND IT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN HYPOTHETICAL: fog is common on Mount Stone's upper mountain and multiple parties have lost the route and ended up in unplanned harder terrain, and in cloud the true south summit is confused with the Middle and North summits. Count your summits and do not accept the first one.

EXIT NOTE THAT IS PART OF THE PLAN, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: the standard finish continues southwest half a mile to the Lake of the Angels basin and out the Putvin Trail — a DIFFERENT trailhead about 4 road miles from Lena Lake. Arrange a shuttle or stash a bike before you start.
hazards: Extensive off-trail and way-trail route-finding over multiple ridges and passes
Loose glacial moraine of all sizes near St. Peter's Gate
A very long outing, up to about 16 miles and 9,000 ft of gain, with limited bail options partway through
Fog and whiteout navigation on Mount Stone's upper mountain — multiple parties have lost the route
Exposed headwall sections with several-hundred-foot drops near the Lena Lake / Lake of the Angels transition, some using a fixed handline or tree roots
Unbridged stream crossings requiring downclimbing to the bed and back out
The exit is at a different trailhead and needs a shuttle

approach_variants.name: Putvin Trail to Lake of the Angels, then west to the saddle north of Point 5945
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, and this peak holds avalanche-capable snow in its upper gullies later than most — slides have been reported in August and September
approach_variants.notes:
THIS IS THE STANDARD APPROACH AND THE ROW'S WAYPOINT LIST DESCRIBES A DIFFERENT ONE — see _DEFECTS. Guidebook and trip-report sources are consistent that Mount Skokomish's standard route goes via the Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels.

The Putvin Trailhead (Trail #813) is on Hamma Hamma Road (FR-25), about 11.8-12.1 miles west of US-101, just past the lower Lena Lake trailhead across a concrete bridge, at roughly 1,600 ft. The trail is unmaintained for its last stretch but well-travelled and easy to follow when snow-free — steep, narrow, unstable footing in places through forest. Around 1.5-2 miles it breaks into the open grassy Whitehorse Creek basin, then climbs to Lake of the Angels at about 4,850-4,920 ft, roughly 3.5 miles and 2,800-3,000 ft of gain, 2-2.5 hours at a moderate pace. That is the last reliable water and the standard camp.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
STAND AT LAKE OF THE ANGELS AND THE CIRQUE ITSELF TELLS YOU WHICH WAY TO GO: MOUNT STONE IS ON YOUR RIGHT, ANOTHER PEAK IS ON YOUR LEFT, AND MOUNT SKOKOMISH IS STRAIGHT AHEAD. That three-way check is the arrival test, and it fixes your orientation before you leave the lake.

THE TURN IS AROUND THE RIGHT-HAND SIDE OF THE LAKE, on a way trail heading WEST to the ridge. Then take a broad gully SOUTHWEST and up toward the SADDLE JUST NORTH OF POINT 5945. That is the base of the climb and it is a named, mapped point — the saddle you want is the one immediately north of 5945, not the next gap along. A map point is the strongest thing you can navigate to in cloud, which is why it is quoted here rather than a description of the terrain.

SECOND TEST, past the saddle: the route does not go straight up from it. From the saddle a boot path contours SOUTH and SOUTHWEST across scree, grass and rock benches around the EAST and SOUTH flanks of the peak, PASSING A LARGE TARN. The tarn is the confirmation. TURN RIGHT AND START CLIMBING WHEN YOU ARE ABOVE THE LARGE TARN — that is the published trigger, and it works because a tarn is a thing you stand beside rather than a thing you see from a distance. Turning up before the tarn puts you on the steeper cliffy ground on the north side of the upper mountain.

THIRD TEST, near the top: the final ground passes through rock bands and scrubby trees across a section known as the hanging or fingertip traverse, then goes up and around LEFT to the true summit, which is large and broad. This peak has THREE SUMMIT HORNS and parties have mistaken a lower false summit for the true south high point. A broad top is the right one; a narrow horn is not.

EXPLICIT WARNING FROM A TRIP REPORT, and it is directional: contouring too far RIGHT (north) near the ridge crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Cut WEST over the ridge instead.
hazards: Notoriously rotten, loose rock throughout the upper mountain and summit scramble — test holds
Steep snow-filled gullies below the summit saddle carry avalanche and sluffing potential well into summer, with August and September slides reported
An exposed hanging or fingertip traverse section near the true summit
Three summit horns, and a false one has fooled parties
The narrow, eroded lower Putvin tread, and the root-and-rock headwall on it
Mountain goats near Lake of the Angels and the peak's base

approach_variants.name: Mildred Lakes Trail from Hamma Hamma Road, the west-side approach
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the off-trail brush above the lakes is much easier with lingering snow cover
approach_variants.notes:
RECORDED BECAUSE THE ROW'S OWN WAYPOINTS DESCRIBE THIS APPROACH, not because it is the standard one. It is a real approach into the Skokomish-Cruiser-Lincoln group, and it is the usual way to Mount Cruiser and Mount Lincoln.

From the Mildred Lakes trailhead on Hamma Hamma Road, the trail drops into a brushy ravine to ford HUCKLEBERRY CREEK at about 2,000 ft near 1.4 miles — the last reliable water before the hard part, and easy to lose in poor light. It then gains roughly 1,000 ft in about half a mile on hand-and-foot ROOT AND ROCK LADDERS, one pitch near 75-80 degrees, to a ridge high point at about 4,100 ft near 2.5 miles. From the ridge the trail drops about 250 ft to Lower Mildred Lake and continues past Middle to Upper Mildred Lake in a wooded bowl between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser at about 3,850 ft near 4.3 miles, with informal camps on rock benches and the last dependable water before going off-trail.

Above the lakes the route leaves the lakeshore path entirely into slide-alder and heather bushwhacking that neighbouring-peak accounts describe as very brushy, climbing to an open basin and connecting saddle beneath Skokomish's south peak at about 5,500 ft.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE ON THIS SIDE IS THE OPEN BASIN AND SADDLE BENEATH THE SOUTH PEAK AT ABOUT 5,500 FT, AND THE TEST FOR IT IS UNDERFOOT: THE FOOTING TURNS TO LOOSE, ROTTEN ROCK FROM THERE UP. Below the saddle you are fighting brush and heather; at and above it you are on scree and shattered rock. That transition is the arrival cue and it does not require seeing anything.

THE TEST FOR THE APPROACH ITSELF IS THE ROOT LADDER, because it is the one unmistakable feature on this trail: about a thousand feet of hand-and-foot climbing on roots and rock in roughly half a mile, one pitch near vertical, topping out on a ridge at about 4,100 ft. If you have not used your hands, you are not on the Mildred Lakes trail. And the trail then DESCENDS off that ridge to the lakes — a trail that keeps climbing past 4,100 ft is not this one.

HONEST LIMIT, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS VARIANT IS SECOND: the ground between the Mildred Lakes and Skokomish's south peak is unmaintained, brushy and easy to lose, with no marker sequence published for it. Guidebook and trip-report sources put the standard route on the Putvin side. Take this approach only if you have a reason to be at the Mildred Lakes, and expect to navigate rather than to follow.
hazards: Unmaintained, brushy, easy-to-lose way-paths above the lakes requiring off-trail navigation
Root and rock ladders on the approach trail, one pitch near vertical, dangerous when wet
Slide-alder bushwhacking that is far worse without snow cover
The same rotten upper-mountain rock and avalanche-capable gullies as the standard side
Post-fire hazards — standing dead and burned trees, rockfall and landslides — in the Bear Gulch Fire closure area

approach_variants.name: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 over Baldy and along the crest
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. North-facing gullies on the last stretch hold steep snow into July
approach_variants.notes:
There is no roadside access to this ridge; the drive only gets you to the trailhead at the end of FR-2860-120, off FR-2870 / Lost Mountain Road, itself off Palo Alto Road south of US-101 near Sequim. Road-end parking at a dirt berm, about 3,300 ft, Northwest Forest Pass required.

Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 leaves the berm on an old roadbed and crosses Mueller Creek almost immediately — the last easy reliable water for a long stretch, so fill up. The trail narrows to single-track around 0.3 mile and then turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 3,000 ft in a little over two miles of fall-line tread with essentially no switchbacks, in places barely a boot-width across eroded crumbly ravine crossings and slopes of packed dirt and shattered shale. It is a climber's path, not a graded trail.

At about 2.7 miles and 5,400-6,200 ft it tops out on the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy, where a short steep side path drops off the crest to a snowmelt spring — the last dependable water on the route.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE CLIMB BEGINS WHERE THE TREAD ENDS, AND THE ARRIVAL TEST IS THE SADDLE BETWEEN TYLER PEAK AND BALDY. You know you are there because the trail stops going up in a line and the ground opens on both sides — navigation shifts from following tread to reading a ridge. There is also a signed Olympic National Park boundary marker in a saddle on this stretch and a spring path dropping off the crest. From here on you are on the crest and the crest is the route.

THE TEST THAT ACTUALLY MATTERS ON THIS ROUTE IS AT THE FAR END, AND IT IS A FALSE SUMMIT WITH A NAME AND A NUMBER: POINT 7076. From below, 7076 reads as the summit. It is not. The true summit of Gray Wolf is 7,218 ft and it lies FURTHER NORTH along the crest and is HIGHER. So the fog rule is simple: after Baldy you drop about 600 ft, climb back up over a prominent bump, and THAT BUMP IS NOT THE TOP. Keep going north over the last of the talus, detouring briefly round the occasional gendarme, and finish with a short Class 2-3 scramble on loose rock. If you turned round on the first big bump past Baldy, you turned round on 7076.

SECOND TEST, on the way to 7076 itself: the crest gets steeper and broken approaching it. The published avoidance is to TRAVERSE WEST at about 6,500 ft and then swing back to gain 7076 by its NORTHWEST aspect, and to stay in the basin below and RIGHT of the broken rock ridge until you can gain the saddle between the twin summits — 7076 has twin tops with snowfields between them. There is no trail at these decision points, which is why they are written down.

THIRD TEST, earlier: Point 6537 is a rocky gendarme and false summit below Baldy, normally SKIRTED ON ITS SOUTH SIDE rather than climbed over. If you are scrambling straight over a tower before you have reached Baldy, you have taken the crest too literally.

HONEST LIMIT: long stretches of this crest are unmarked and off-trail and the whole thing is above treeline. Carry a map or GPS; the ridge is the handrail but the summit identification is not obvious by eye.
hazards: Sudden fast-moving whiteouts and lightning on an open above-treeline ridge with miles of exposure
Loose shale and scree with occasional exposed steps along the crest
Lingering steep snowfields in north-facing gullies into July, warranting an ice axe
No reliable water once past the Baldy saddle spring
Long unmarked ridge navigation with route-finding around gendarmes and false summits
The Gray Wolf River bridge on the alternative approach is out — a required and hazardous ford at high water
Bear canister required within Olympic National Park

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin and the east face, for a traverse rather than an out-and-back
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The other end of the same ridge, and the reason to know it is that it turns this route into a traverse instead of a there-and-back over Baldy twice. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, the Royal Basin Trail leads to Royal Lake and Upper Royal Basin. From the ridge, the east face drops roughly 3,000 ft to intersect the Royal Basin Trail.

It is steep, loose and only lightly travelled: packed dirt and shattered shale, brushy notches, and picking through timber looking for blazes and cairns. Some parties scree-ski the looser upper sections rather than rope up at all. It is not a bolted or standardised line — where parties do rope down a short cliffy step, anchors are improvised from trees or natural rock horns.

Most commonly this is used as the EXIT after climbing from Maynard Burn, closing a loop out Royal Basin or back over the ridge.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
USED AS AN APPROACH, THE ARRIVAL TEST IS GAINING THE CREST — and this side has no marker sequence for doing it, which is the honest state of the record. Trip reports describe finding blazes and cairns through timber rather than following a line. Treat it as navigation, not route-following.

THE SUMMIT TESTS ONCE ON THE CREST ARE THE SAME AND THEY ARE THE VALUABLE PART: POINT 7076 IS A FALSE SUMMIT. Coming from the Royal Basin side you meet the true 7,218 ft summit from the north-east rather than from the south, so the trap runs the other way — the bump you must not stop on lies SOUTH of the true summit on this approach. Fix which side of you 7076 should be before you commit to the crest in cloud.

HONEST LIMIT AND A RECOMMENDATION: this variant is documented as a descent far more thoroughly than as an ascent, and the sources give no fixed, repeatable rappel count for the cliffy step — expect at most one or two short rappels well under 60 m if you choose to rope, and expect most parties to downclimb or scree-ski instead. Confirm current conditions against a recent trip report before relying on it either way.
hazards: Steep, loose, lightly travelled ground with no established line and improvised anchors if roped
Roughly 3,000 ft of descent or ascent on packed dirt and shattered shale
Brushy notches and timber navigation looking for blazes and cairns
Committing: once on the east face there is no easy return to the crest
Every ridge-crest hazard above, in a longer day

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness and Royal Basin, over the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep. The notch below the divide holds 35-40 degree snow and an axe is worth carrying outside late season
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead on FR-2870 — large parking area, vault toilet, self-issue Olympic National Park wilderness permit at the kiosk — take Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 about a mile. The trail forks just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge; BEAR RIGHT onto the Royal Basin Trail #832. The Maynard Burn Trail continues straight and is easy to mistake in early light.

Royal Creek Camp at about 3.4 miles is a common first night. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the main basecamp, with designated sites and a seasonal ranger post — the last dependable water before the dry climb. Many parties push on to camps around 5,800-6,200 ft in upper Royal Basin.

From upper Royal Basin, climb a moraine and a snowfield of roughly 35-40 degrees to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend shower-tile scree to grass and heather benches above Deception Basin.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS THE LOWER LEFT CORNER OF THE MYSTERY GLACIER, AND THE THING THAT MARKS IT IS A LAKE YOU CANNOT MISTAKE FOR ANYTHING ELSE: A JADE-GREEN MORAINE-BOUNDED LAKE SITS AT THE GLACIER'S BASE. Drop off the benches into Deception Basin, cross a dark moraine, and the lake is at the foot of the ice. Get on the glacier at its LOWER LEFT corner. Colour is a fog-usable marker at short range and there is one such lake here.

THE TEST FOR THE GLACIER CROSSING IS A DIAGONAL: you enter at the lower LEFT and exit at the upper RIGHT, at a COL at about 6,700 ft on the peak's EAST side. The ice is stagnant and low-angle with a few small crevasses to step over — this is a walk with a rope on, not a serious glacier. If you are climbing straight up the fall line rather than trending right, you are not heading for the col.

SECOND TEST, above the col, and it is a specific distance and a specific side: from the col traverse mixed rock and snow to reach OPEN SNOW ABOUT 200 FT SOUTH OF THE COL, then climb those slopes STAYING SOUTH OF the blocky rock band immediately above. South of the rock band, not through it. Snow angles reach around 40 degrees and take pickets well. The gullies feeding this section are where the rockfall comes from, so move one at a time and keep the party to three or fewer.

THIRD TEST, and it is the commitment point: a short CLASS 4 STEP on poor rock, with steep runout dirt below it, gains a NOTCH NEAR 7,500 FT. Trend CLIMBER'S LEFT on the approach to it. This step has to be downclimbed on the way out, usually unroped, and one party rated a single move on the reverse at 5.8 — so it is worth being certain about before you commit. A moat over 30 ft deep has been reported below the gully late in the season, which changes how the section is entered and exited.

WHAT CONFIRMS YOU ARE THROUGH: beyond the notch a clean Class 3 gully leads to the summit block, and THE ROCK GETS MARKEDLY BETTER than anything below it. Good rock on this peak means you are nearly there.
hazards: Rotten, tilted pillow basalt that breaks away readily, with rockfall funnelled by the gullies above the col
A Class 4 step on poor rock over steep runout dirt that must be reversed on descent — one party graded a move on the downclimb at 5.8
A reported moat over 30 ft deep below the gully late in the season
Lingering steep snow on the approach gullies and Mystery Glacier into summer, and a 35-40 degree snow slope below the Royal-Deception notch
Remote terrain — a solo traveller died in a fall near the peak's south end in July 2022

approach_variants.name: Home Lake and Constance Pass, reaching Deception Basin from the south
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The other side, and the one that suits a party already camped at Home Lake for Fricaba or Warrior. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead, Trail #833.2 to Camp Handy at about 3.4 miles and Boulder Shelter at about 6.4 miles and 4,890 ft, then the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail to Home Lake at roughly 9.3 miles and 5,308-5,330 ft. From camp, climbers' paths lead up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, and from there the route traverses and descends west into upper Deception Basin.

This is the same basin the Royal Basin parties drop into, reached from the opposite end. It is the approach a high-route party is already on, and one detailed account describes exiting this way over Gunsight Pass toward Constance Pass and out the Dosewallips and Del Monte Ridge trail system with no rappels — a valid variant exit, distinct from reversing the ascent.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
IDENTICAL ONCE YOU ARE IN DECEPTION BASIN, and the shared test is the good one: the JADE-GREEN MORAINE-BOUNDED LAKE at the foot of the Mystery Glacier. Get on the ice at its LOWER LEFT corner and cross diagonally to the COL AT ABOUT 6,700 FT at its UPPER RIGHT, on the peak's EAST side.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is at Constance Pass, because you arrive at Deception Basin along its length rather than dropping into its head. Leave the maintained trail at the pass and work WEST and DOWN into the upper basin. Loose scree on the descent is normal here. If you are contouring without losing height you have not committed to the basin; if you are climbing again you have crossed it and are heading for the Fricaba-Hal Foss ridge instead.

ABOVE THE COL THE TESTS ARE THE SAME: open snow about 200 ft SOUTH of the col, climbed staying SOUTH of the blocky rock band; then a short Class 4 step approached CLIMBER'S LEFT to a notch near 7,500 ft; then a clean Class 3 gully on markedly better rock to the summit.
hazards: Loose scree traverses between Constance Pass and Deception Basin
All the summit-block hazards of the standard variant, including the reversible Class 4 step
Steep snow lingering on the Constance Pass and Deception Basin traverse into July
Long committing backcountry travel far from help

approach_variants.name: Upper Dungeness Trail to Home Lake and Constance Pass
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct per NPS guidance for the Constance Pass and Home Lake corridor; earlier trips should expect lingering snow
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead at about 2,880 ft at the end of FR 2870, follow Upper Dungeness Trail #833.2 south along the Dungeness River. The first mile is mostly flat; STAY LEFT at the Royal Basin Trail junction near a mile. Camp Handy — riverside meadow with a cedar shingle shelter — comes at about 3.4 miles.

Just past Camp Handy the trail forks; take the UPHILL fork and begin a sustained, largely switchback-free climb of about 3 miles and 1,800 ft to Boulder Shelter at 6.4 miles and about 4,890 ft. The creek there is the most reliable water on the whole approach — treat it as the last sure fill-up. Bear right at the shelter onto the Home Lake / Constance Pass Trail. The park boundary is about a mile beyond, after which brush closes in from both sides.

The final 2.9 miles to Home Lake at 5,330 ft, roughly 9.3-9.6 miles from the trailhead, climb another 700-900 ft through subalpine forest into heather meadows, crossing two or three small streams; one waterfall crossing is awkward to keep feet dry and is slick with a full pack early season. Home Lake is the standard basecamp for Fricaba, Hal Foss, Mystery and Deception.

From camp continue on climbers' paths — no maintained tread — up to Constance Pass at about 5,750-5,800 ft, then traverse and descend west into upper Deception Basin.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS THE COL BETWEEN FRICABA AND HAL FOSS, AND THE PUBLISHED TEST FOR IT IS THE ONE THING ABOUT THIS PEAK THAT WORKS WITHOUT SEEING ANYTHING: FROM DECEPTION BASIN, ASCEND EASTWARD AIMING FOR THE LOWEST POINT IN THE RIDGE CONNECTING FRICABA WITH HAL FOSS. Lowest point. Not the nearest gully, not the most obvious scree fan — the lowest saddle on that connecting ridge. In cloud you can still tell which way a skyline sags by walking toward the direction the ground stops climbing soonest.

SECOND TEST, once at the col: turn AWAY from Hal Foss and follow the ridge up to Fricaba. The North and SW ridges are the two most readily ascended and this is the SW one. The first 500 to 600 vertical feet off the pass is the STEEPEST part of the climb; after that it eases into a straightforward scree hike. So the shape of the effort is a check on the line: steep first, easy after. A route that stays uniformly moderate is not this one.

THIRD TEST, AND IT IS WHICH SUMMIT: FRICABA'S SW PEAK IS THE TRUE, HIGHER TOP. The NE peak lies about half a mile away along the NE ridge and is noticeably lower. If you have walked half a mile of ridge from the top you reached and are now standing somewhere higher, you were on the NE peak.

WHAT THE GROUND FEELS LIKE, so it does not read as a wrong turn: Fricaba is extremely shattered, rotten shale. Two steps up and one slide back is the normal experience, not evidence you are off route. Brief Class 2-3 scrambling appears near the ridge crest.
hazards: Extremely shattered rotten shale with real rockfall and ankle-turn hazard the whole way up
Loose talus and scree on the upper slopes, with the steepest 500-600 ft immediately off the pass
Lingering steep snow on the Constance Pass to Deception Basin traverse into July, warranting an axe
Brief exposed Class 3 downclimbing near the ridge crest and col on the way out
A long, committing backcountry approach far from help
Boulder Shelter sits at the foot of an avalanche chute with snapped trees in the scar

approach_variants.name: Royal Basin and the Royal-Deception divide into Deception Basin
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
The other way into the same basin, and the one that suits a party doing Fricaba alongside Mystery and Deception. From the Upper Dungeness Trailhead take Trail #833.2 about a mile and BEAR RIGHT onto the Royal Basin Trail #832 at the fork just before the Royal Creek footlog bridge. Royal Lake at about 7.2 miles and 5,100 ft is the basecamp; upper Royal Basin camps sit around 5,800-6,200 ft.

From upper Royal Basin climb the moraine and a 35-40 degree snowfield to the notch on the Royal-Deception divide at about 6,500-6,560 ft, then descend scree to the grass and heather benches above Deception Basin. Fricaba is then across the basin to the east.

One published day-2 description of this side has parties angling up toward the pass going east for Fricaba, then round to the LEFT of some gendarmes and up a steep scree route the account calls self-explanatory.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
SAME BASE, SAME TEST, APPROACHED ACROSS THE BASIN RATHER THAN DOWN INTO IT: from Deception Basin, ascend EASTWARD aiming for the LOWEST POINT IN THE RIDGE CONNECTING FRICABA WITH HAL FOSS.

THE EXTRA TEST THIS SIDE NEEDS is the gendarmes on the way up: the published line goes round them to the LEFT, then up steep scree. If you are scrambling over towers rather than skirting them, you have taken the crest instead of the scree.

AND THE SAME SUMMIT TEST: THE SW PEAK IS THE TRUE TOP. The NE peak, half a mile off along the NE ridge, is lower.

HONEST LIMIT: the scree route above the col is described in the sources as self-explanatory, which is another way of saying nobody has written down a marker for it. It is a walk-up on rubbish rock; the navigation problem is getting to the col, not what happens above it.
hazards: A 35-40 degree snowfield below the Royal-Deception notch, wanting an axe outside late season
Shattered shale and scree on Fricaba itself
Gendarmes on the approach ridge that must be skirted rather than climbed
Long approach with the last dependable water at Royal Lake

approach_variants.name: Upper Trailhead on NFR 24, Trail #812 summer route
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Oct for the snow-free summer trail; outside that the chute fills and the upper switchbacks are buried
approach_variants.notes:
From the Upper Trailhead at about 3,500 ft, at the end of FS Road 2419-014 off FS 24 / FS 2419 — vault toilet, picnic table, Northwest Forest Pass required — Trail #812 climbs immediately. The first 0.3 mile is stacked stairstep switchbacks through forest, merging with the longer lower-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft.

From the merge, continue up the south ridge through increasingly open forest to timberline at about 4,500 ft, roughly a mile in. In summer conditions the trail is snow-free and well cut essentially to the top, switchbacking across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly subalpine meadows, threading a narrow notch and crossing west-facing slopes to the 5,944 ft summit. Total gain from the Upper Trailhead is 2,444 ft over 1.6 miles one way. No water on the upper route; carry all you need.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE DECISION POINT ON THIS MOUNTAIN IS A SIGNED JUNCTION AT TIMBERLINE, ROUGHLY 4,500 FT, AND A SIGN IS THE BEST FOG MARKER THERE IS BECAUSE IT DOES NOT DEPEND ON VISIBILITY BEYOND ARM'S LENGTH. At that junction the WINTER CLIMBING ROUTE BREAKS RIGHT, straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute, and the MAINTAINED SUMMER TRAIL SWITCHBACKS LEFT across rock-strewn slopes and gravelly meadows. This variant is the LEFT one.

If you find yourself climbing a single steep funnel-shaped gully rather than working a series of switchbacks, you have taken the right-hand branch and you are on the winter route.

SECOND TEST, higher: the summer trail threads a NARROW NOTCH and then crosses WEST-FACING slopes before the final approach to the summit. Many of its switchbacks have stairstep risers built into them. Built steps are man-made and unambiguous underfoot. If you are on trackless scree you have left the trail.

HONEST LIMIT, AND IT IS SEASONAL RATHER THAN NAVIGATIONAL: outside roughly November to June, snow fills the chute and buries the upper switchbacks, and most parties then climb the chute directly because the summer trail is not there to be found. That is not a route-finding failure; it is a different route, and it demands an ice axe and traction. The rocks in and bordering the chute are notoriously slick when wet even outside full winter conditions — that is an official Forest Service warning, not a trip-report opinion.
hazards: The southeast-facing chute is an avalanche funnel that becomes sun-soaked and prone to wet slides by early-mid afternoon — start early and check NWAC in spring
Chute-bordering rocks are extremely slick when wet or in fog
Losing the trail under snow leads onto steeper, looser ground
A very popular and crowded trail with kicked-loose rock from parties above
No water on route
Fragile subalpine vegetation on the open upper slopes

approach_variants.name: Lower Trailhead, the long approach to the same trail
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Oct, and it is snow-free earlier than the upper road in some years
approach_variants.notes:
The Lower Trailhead sits at about 2,600 ft, 3.1 miles one way, and takes no fee. It welcomes you with an easy grade rather than the upper trailhead's near-immediate jolt, and it is the sensible choice when FS Road 2419-014 to the upper lot is snowed in or gated.

It climbs steadily through forest and joins the upper-trailhead trail at roughly 3,900 ft. Everything above the merge is identical.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE FIRST TEST IS THE MERGE AT ABOUT 3,900 FT, where the lower trail joins the upper-trailhead trail. From below, that junction is the confirmation you are on the right path at all; from above it is the fork you take DOWNHILL to get back to the lower lot rather than the upper one. Parties have descended to the wrong car here.

THE DECISION POINT IS THE SAME SIGNED JUNCTION AT TIMBERLINE, ROUGHLY 4,500 FT, about 2.5 miles from the lower trailhead: the WINTER CLIMBING ROUTE BREAKS RIGHT up the chute, the SUMMER TRAIL SWITCHBACKS LEFT. Take the left.

AND THE SAME CONFIRMATIONS ABOVE IT: stairstep risers built into the switchbacks, a narrow notch, and west-facing slopes before the summit.
hazards: Same as the upper-trailhead variant, over a longer and gentler approach
The 3,900 ft merge is where parties descend to the wrong trailhead
No water on the upper route

approach_variants.name: The winter chute, direct from the timberline junction
approach_variants.season: Roughly Nov-Jun, while the chute holds a firm continuous snowpack
approach_variants.notes:
Not a different trailhead but a genuinely different climb, and it is what most parties are on outside core summer because the summer switchbacks are buried. From either trailhead, follow Trail #812 to the signed timberline junction at about 4,500 ft and take the right-hand branch straight up the prominent scree-and-snow chute below the summit saddle.

This demands an ice axe and traction — crampons or microspikes — and it is steep, funnel-shaped slide-path terrain with real avalanche potential. Check avalanche conditions before going up.

It is also the fast descent when conditions allow: with an axe carried in self-arrest position, parties glissade roughly 1,000 ft in a couple of minutes. That is consequential terrain rather than a casual slide.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE IS THE SIGNED TIMBERLINE JUNCTION AT ABOUT 4,500 FT AND THE RIGHT-HAND BRANCH OUT OF IT. That is the whole test and it is the same sign the summer parties turn left at. The chute is the prominent scree-and-snow funnel that runs straight up toward the summit saddle from there — there is one, it is obvious, and it is the reason the junction is signed at all.

THE CONFIRMING TEST IS THAT THE GROUND STOPS SWITCHBACKING. The summer trail traverses; the chute goes up the fall line. If you are still zig-zagging you took the left branch.

THE TEST FOR WHETHER YOU SHOULD BE THERE AT ALL, which matters more on this route than finding it: the chute is south-east facing and sun-soaked, and by early-to-mid afternoon in spring it is prone to wet slides. Start early. Later in the season, as the snow thins and exposes talus, rock and ice bulges, the chute stops being the fast line and becomes the dangerous one — at that point the correct call is the summer switchbacks for the whole descent.
hazards: A steep funnel-shaped slide path with real avalanche potential; check NWAC before going
Wet-slide danger by early-mid afternoon in spring on a sun-soaked southeast aspect
Exposed rocks and ice bulges lower in the chute as snow thins — glissading then becomes dangerous
An uncontrolled glissade or a fall on hard snow without self-arrest skill on genuinely consequential terrain
Slick chute-bordering rocks when wet or in fog

approach_variants.name: FR-2419 up the Big Creek drainage to the road-end trailhead
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep, best Jul-Aug. Spring and early summer put avalanche-capable snow in the gully
approach_variants.notes:
From the T-intersection at the end of North Lake Cushman Road, go right onto FS Road 24 for about a mile, then left onto FS Road 2419 and follow it up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to its end at a small trailhead at about 3,026 ft. Self-issue Mt. Skokomish Wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass at the kiosk.

From here the trail quickly becomes a boot path and then largely off-trail scrambling — there is no numbered maintained trail for most of the route. It climbs directly and steeply through forest, hand-over-hand on roots and rock in places, to a couple of open meadow benches around 3,800 ft. That meadow band holds the most reliable early-season water via snowmelt seeps; by mid-to-late summer expect it dry, so carry what you need from the car.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ROUTE IS A SEQUENCE OF THREE TERRAIN CHANGES AND EACH ONE IS A CHECK YOU CAN MAKE WITHOUT SEEING ANYTHING. First: forest gives way to OPEN MEADOW BENCHES around 3,800 ft — that is where the ridgeline and neighbouring Mount Ellinor come into view on a clear day, and where the ground briefly eases. Second: above the meadows you enter SCREE AND TALUS and the rule is to stay primarily on the CLIMBER'S-LEFT side of a large loose rocky gully. Left side of the gully, all the way. Third: the path winds above the gully until it GAINS THE SOUTHERN RIDGELINE, and from there the ground drops away on BOTH sides.

THE ARRIVAL TEST FOR THE REAL CLIMBING IS THE SOUTH SADDLE AT ABOUT 5,950 FT, AND IT HAS TWO MARKERS: it is a KNOWN BIVY SITE, and it is the FIRST POINT ON THE ROUTE WHERE THE TRUE SUMMIT BECOMES VISIBLE. Flat ground you could sleep on, high on a ridge, is a thing you can identify by standing on it.

SECOND TEST, above the saddle: a STONE WIND SHELTER sits on the ridge. A built structure is unambiguous in any weather. From the wind shelter a final short Class 3-4 scramble gains the true 6,255 ft summit. If you have topped out without passing a stone shelter, you are on the false summit below it.

THE SECTION IN BETWEEN IS THE ONE PEOPLE REMEMBER: the ridge-crest traverse called the Dog Walk Ledge or the Catwalk, where in several spots the tread narrows to barely one boot-width with real exposure on both sides. Class 3 with a couple of Class 3+/4 moves. If the crest you are on is comfortably wide the whole way, you have not reached it yet.

WHAT GOING TOO FAR LOOKS LIKE: a trip report warns specifically that contouring too far RIGHT (north) near the crest gets sketchy, exposed and dangerous. Stay left of the drop-off on the north side.
hazards: Loose rock and rockfall in the entry gullies and on the talus — spread the group out rather than stacking above and below
Sustained exposure on the Dog Walk Ledge / Catwalk, where the tread is one boot wide with drops on both sides
Steep avalanche-prone snow in the gullies and on the saddle in spring and early season
The scree field below the false summit is greasy and slick when wet
Significant elevation loss on descent, hard on knees and ankles, and slower than the climb
Route-finding through the forested lower section, meadows and talus in poor visibility
Little shade above treeline; the route gets hot

approach_variants.name: From Mount Ellinor, across the connecting ridge or the west-side basin
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
Recorded as an approach because parties do reach Washington from Ellinor rather than from Big Creek, usually as half of a traverse. Ellinor is reached by Trail #812 from its Upper or Lower Trailhead, both on the same North Lake Cushman Road corridor, and from Ellinor's summit the connecting ridge runs northeast toward Washington.

It is not a walk. The crest is fractured, weathered pillow basalt with sustained Class 4 scrambling past a series of gendarmes, and it carries a loose 50 ft downclimb that most accounts call the least enjoyable part of the day. The alternative that several sources prefer is the west-side basin traverse: drop into the basin below the crest and cross it, rejoining Ellinor's standard winter route line rather than fighting the ridge.

Used as an approach to Washington this is a long way round for a peak with a 3.2 km trail of its own, and it is here for traverse parties.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
COMING FROM ELLINOR THE ARRIVAL TEST FOR WASHINGTON'S SUMMIT GROUND IS THE SAME STONE WIND SHELTER on the ridge, with the final short Class 3-4 scramble above it to the 6,255 ft top.

THE TEST ON THE CONNECTING RIDGE ITSELF, WHICH IS WHERE THE DAY IS DECIDED: hidden ledges keep the difficulty at Class 4 or below on most of the gendarmes, so if you are pulling harder than that you have taken the crest where a ledge existed. Look below the obvious line before committing to it. Where the ridge gets too difficult or exposed to continue unroped, the published answer is to DROP INTO THE BASIN BELOW and either downclimb a technical sequence or bypass it on a snow finger.

HONEST LIMIT: the guidebook-level advice on the crux gendarme downclimb is to avoid it — the rock is notably poor and the exposure severe, and several sources recommend the west-side basin instead of the direct ridge. That is a recommendation to change route, not a marker, and this variant is written down mainly so a party knows the option exists before they are standing on it.
hazards: Fractured, weathered pillow basalt on the connecting ridge with a crux gendarme downclimb of notably poor rock and severe exposure
Sustained Class 4 scrambling past gendarmes with a loose 50 ft downclimb
Committing terrain between two summits with no quick exit
All the Washington summit-ridge hazards at the end of it

approach_variants.name: FR-2419 past the second Big Creek crossing, the way trail to the Shield Wall
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
From US 101 turn west onto Lake Cushman Road and in about 1.5 miles turn right onto Forest Road 2419. Continue up the Big Creek drainage to just past the SECOND CROSSING OF BIG CREEK, at about 3,100 ft. This is NOT the standard route's trailhead: the way trail for this route leaves the road roughly 1,000 ft BEYOND the standard route's trail entrance, so if you have parked where everybody else parks, you are in the wrong place by a thousand feet of road.

Follow an old roadbed across Big Creek and a climbers' trail up a rock rib, gaining roughly 1,600 ft toward the bowl below the Shield Wall. A small way trail leads to the base of the large rock section of the southeast ridge at about 3,700 ft; bear RIGHT (east) around those rocks and follow the ridgeline until you are forced RIGHT (north) by prominent gendarmes. A gully then ascends up and left to a notch at the wall's LEFT corner at about 4,850 ft, where the technical climbing begins.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE ARRIVAL TEST IS A NOTCH AT THE LEFT-HAND CORNER OF THE WALL AT ABOUT 4,850 FT, AND THE THING THAT PROVES IT BEYOND ARGUMENT IS BOLTS. This route's first pitch carries TWO FIXED BOLTS mid-pitch and a BOLTED BELAY STATION at its top. That is the only fixed hardware on the lower mountain and it is on this pitch. So: if you have climbed a rope length and there is no bolt anywhere on it, you are not on the Shield Wall — go back down and find the notch. Bolts are man-made, they do not move with the season, and you can find them by hand.

THE SEQUENCE THAT GETS YOU THERE IS THREE FORCED TURNS AND EACH IS A CHECK: (1) the base of the large rock section of the SE ridge at about 3,700 ft — bear RIGHT, east, AROUND the rocks rather than up them; (2) follow the ridgeline until PROMINENT GENDARMES FORCE YOU RIGHT (north) — you are not choosing to go right, the terrain makes you; (3) the gully then goes UP AND LEFT to the notch. Right, right, then left. If you have made only rightward moves, you have not found the gully.

WHAT WRONG LOOKS LIKE AT THE START: taking the standard route's trail entrance instead of the one a thousand feet further up the road puts you on the walk-up scramble, which is the DESCENT for this climb. That is not a disaster — it is the way down — but it will not deliver you to the Shield Wall.

WHAT CONFIRMS THE ROUTE ABOVE PITCH ONE: the Shield Wall proper is seven pitches of low fifth to 5.7, and the crux is a WELL-PROTECTED FINGER CRACK passing the second tower ON THE RIGHT. On a route where most pitches take only one to five pieces, a pitch that protects well is itself a marker. Above the wall the ridge continues through rock parapets and gendarmes with three 30 m rappels interleaved with about six more pitches of third class to 5.7 to the summit.

DESCENT NOTE THAT BEARS ON THE APPROACH: you come down Mount Washington's standard Class 3-4 scramble to the same FR-2419 trailhead area, so the two trail entrances are a thousand feet apart at the road and you will use both in one day.
hazards: Generally poor rock for much of the route, with only one to five placements available on many pitches
Retreat from partway up is reported as difficult and potentially dangerous — commit only in good weather with a competent party
Loose blocks on the parapets of the upper SE ridge above the Shield Wall proper
Few opportunities to sling horns or blocks despite what older guidebooks suggest
Three rappels interleaved with climbing high on the route, on loose ground
The descent is an exposed Class 3-4 scramble at the end of thirteen pitches

approach_variants.name: Climb Mount Washington first from FR-2419 — the traverse starts on its summit
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jun-Sep
approach_variants.notes:
This route has no trailhead and no approach of its own. It begins on Mount Washington's summit and runs southwest along the connecting ridge to Mount Ellinor, rather than descending Washington's standard route.

So the approach is Washington's standard south route: FS Road 24 off North Lake Cushman Road for about a mile, left onto FS Road 2419 and up the Big Creek drainage roughly 6.6 miles to the road-end trailhead at about 3,026 ft; steep boot path through forest to the meadow benches; scree and talus staying climber's-left of the large loose gully; the southern ridgeline and the exposed Dog Walk Ledge; the scree field below the false summit and the goat trail up its climber's-right edge to the stone wind shelter; and a final short Class 3-4 scramble to the 6,255 ft summit.

Most parties finish at Ellinor and walk out its standard trail from the upper trailhead, which is a different parking area on the same road corridor — plan the shuttle. Reversing the traverse back over Washington is possible but nobody recommends it.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THIS ROUTE IS A SUMMIT, AND THE TEST THAT YOU ARE ON THE RIGHT ONE IS A BUILDING: you passed a STONE WIND SHELTER on the ridge just below and then made a short Class 3-4 scramble to a top with a summit register on it. If you have not passed a stone shelter, you are on Washington's false summit and the traverse has not started.

THE TEST THAT YOU ARE ON THE TRAVERSE AND NOT ON A DESCENT IS THE FIRST FEATURE, AND IT IS THE BEST SECTION OF THE ROUTE RATHER THAN THE WORST: from the summit, follow the narrow crest of fractured pillow basalt SOUTHWEST. The first thing you meet is THE WEDGE, about 150 ft of POSITIVE low-fifth / Class 4 climbing on good holds. Positive holds on this mountain are unusual enough to be diagnostic. If the first 150 ft off the summit feels loose and unpleasant and you are losing height fast, you have dropped off the crest into the standard descent gully instead of onto the ridge.

SECOND TEST, further along: past the Wedge the ridge continues as sustained Class 4 past a series of gendarmes, and HIDDEN LEDGES usually keep the difficulty at Class 4 or below. So if a gendarme is presenting you with fifth-class moves, look below the obvious line before you commit — the ledge is probably there and you have not found it. One loose 50 ft downclimb is the section everybody dislikes; it is part of the route, not a sign you are off it.

THE DECISION POINT: where the crest becomes too hard or too exposed to continue unroped, the published answer is to DROP INTO THE BASIN BELOW and either downclimb a technical sequence or bypass it on a SNOW FINGER, rejoining Ellinor's standard winter route line to that summit. Several sources recommend taking the west-side basin traverse into Ellinor's northeast couloir over the direct ridge from the start, specifically because the crux gendarme downclimb has poor rock and severe exposure.
hazards: Fractured, weathered pillow basalt the whole length of the crest
A crux gendarme downclimb with notably poor rock and severe exposure that guides often advise bypassing entirely
Sustained Class 4 with hidden ledges — the difficulty depends on finding them
A loose 50 ft downclimb
Committing ground between two summits with no quick exit
The exit is at a different trailhead from the start; plan a shuttle

approach_variants.name: South Fork Skokomish Trail #873 to Sundown Pass, then the Six Ridge crest and the Mount Olson Way
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by two fords that are only reliably safe in late summer and early autumn low water
approach_variants.notes:
Mount Olson sees very few ascents and is normally reached as a side trip off the long Six Ridge traverse. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish Trailhead (Trail #873), reached via Skokomish Valley Road, FS-23 and FS-2361 from Shelton — FS-2361 is gated 1 October to 30 April — the trail runs up the valley. There is an unbridged FORD of the South Fork at about 2.4 miles and 1,450 ft that is only ankle-deep and safely crossable in late summer or early autumn low water; at other times it is a serious hazard. The Olympic National Park boundary comes near 5.1 miles, after which tread grows fainter and a self-issue backcountry permit is required.

Sundown Pass, a forested saddle marked by a broken signpost, comes at about 7.2 miles and 4,125 ft — this is the junction with the Six Ridge Trail heading east along the crest. Lake Sundown is a short spur off the pass at about 7.6 miles and 4,030 ft: the last dependable water and the standard basecamp.

Follow the Six Ridge Trail east along its sawtooth crest — a ridge either side with a gully in the middle, and brutal uphill for every downhill — to about 8.7 miles and 4,650 ft, where an unsigned, unofficial boot path known as the MOUNT OLSON WAY leaves the trail for the peak. It is faint and overgrown with blowdown and lingering snowfields into midsummer. A boulder-field tarn at about 5,100 ft below the summit block is the last water and a common bivy.
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS THE PASS IMMEDIATELY EAST OF THE SUMMIT, AND THE TEST IS THAT THE CLIMBING STARTS THE MOMENT YOU STAND IN IT. From the pass, the final ascent to Olson's 5,289 ft top is a steep, unmarked scramble up a GRASSY AND HEATHER SLOPE pitched around 55-60 degrees in places — hands-on, solid Class 3 — directly above you. Grass and heather at that angle is a distinctive surface: it is neither talus nor rock, and you are either on it or you are not.

SECOND TEST, and it is what tells you the slope is easing correctly rather than that you have wandered: the pitch EASES AND CURVES ROUND THE NORTH SIDE of the peak onto a HEATHER BENCH, and then it is an easy stroll to the true summit. So the sequence is steep grass, then a bench that takes you leftward round the peak, then a walk. If the ground stays steep all the way to a top, or if you are on rock and scree rather than heather, you are on the wrong side.

THE APPROACH TEST BEFORE ANY OF THAT is the departure from Six Ridge, because it is the thing people miss: the Mount Olson Way leaves the Six Ridge Trail at the point on the sawtooth crest CLOSEST TO OLSON, at about 4,650 ft, and it is UNSIGNED. It is faint, overgrown and blowdown-choked. If you are still on obvious trail after passing the point where the crest is nearest the peak, you have walked past the turn.

HONEST LIMIT: there is no documented roped climbing route, rack or pitch-by-pitch description for this peak in any source checked — Mountain Project and SummitPost have no page for it, and Peakbagger and Peakery list it without a route write-up. This is a bushwhack and scramble objective for peak-baggers, and the markers above are the sum of what has been written down. Treat the notch and the upper summit meadow as the crux going both ways: both are loose and exposed and better handled with an axe or a pole for self-arrest, especially wet or under late snow.
hazards: Two unbridged fords only safely crossable in late summer and early autumn low water
Route-finding on trail-less and boot-path terrain with an unsigned departure from Six Ridge
Dense brush and blowdown along the Six Ridge approach
A 55-60 degree grass and heather summit pitch that is loose and exposed, and worse descending
FS-2361 is gated 1 October to 30 April
Afternoon weather on an exposed crest, and a multi-day return from a very lightly visited peak

_SKIPPED._note: Three routes with an empty approach_variants were deliberately left empty. An empty result is a real result; each reason is a statement about what is published, not about effort.
_SKIPPED.wa_andersons_thumb_standard: POSITIONED ONLY RELATIVE TO ITS NEIGHBOURS, which the brief rules out as a fog test. The row's own beta says it plainly: Anderson's Thumb has no dedicated guidebook route description and no topo, and the only accounts are trip-report asides from parties climbing Mount Anderson — one pair was tempted to scramble it on the way out from the Anderson Glacier moraine and turned back when heavy rain started. Every published fix on it is of the form 'the prominent pinnacle in the Flypaper Pass / Echo Rock vicinity', i.e. it is located by naming two other features. In cloud a party could reach Flypaper Pass reliably (see the Mount Anderson entry) and would then have nothing at all to tell them which of the rock towers around the col is the Thumb, where its base is, or which side of it goes. Writing a baseFinding here would mean inventing a marker on a pinnacle nobody has described, on rock a single sentence calls 'good sandstone'. The honest state of the record is: this is an optional unrated scramble bolted onto a Mount Anderson trip, identified by eye in good weather.
_SKIPPED.wa_mount_washington_olympic_winter_direc: THE ROUTE'S OWN DOCUMENTATION SAYS THE BASE CANNOT BE FOUND, WHICH IS THE STRONGEST POSSIBLE REASON NOT TO CLAIM OTHERWISE. The line is described as trail walking, bushwhacking and snow travel from Jefferson Pass until 'a hidden gully near the top' gives one pitch of about 180 ft of steep snow and chossy rock. The only detailed account attached to it is a trip report whose author got off track on the ascent from Jefferson Pass and whose advice is to keep trending west toward the drainage rather than heading up — that is a correction to a navigational error, not a marker. A gully described by its own sources as HIDDEN, on an approach where parties are on record getting lost, has no published fog test. It is also a winter route, where the terrain the markers would sit on is under snow. Anything written here would be invention.
_SKIPPED.wa_mount_barnes_scramble: NO PUBLISHED MARKER FOR WHERE THE CLIMBING STARTS. Barnes is a cross-country side trip off the Bailey Range Traverse with no maintained trail to it, and the entire published summit description is that from a camp near Bear Pass or a nearby meadow you contour scree and lingering snow southeast, then curl north on a boot track up a moderate scree slope to a Class 2 top, a few hours round trip. Every noun in that is generic — scree, snow, a boot track, a moderate slope — and none of it distinguishes the correct slope from the several others off that crest. The one fixed thing is Bear Pass itself, and locating a climb by naming the pass a mile away is exactly the neighbour-relative fix the brief excludes. Note also that reaching Barnes at all is the hard part and it is well documented: 'the maze' of slide alder between the Elwha River and Elwha Basin can take hours on a known route, the Elwha Snowfinger has largely melted out and is no longer a dependable ramp, and NPS reported 9 helicopter rescues among roughly 150 permitted Bailey Range parties in 2018. A party on this peak has navigation problems far larger than finding the base, and a fabricated marker would not help with any of them.

_DEFECTS._note: Data defects noticed in passing while reading these rows. Reported, not fixed — this batch writes only approach_variants.
_DEFECTS.duplicate_mount_stone_rows: wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels ('South Route via Lake of the Angels', Class 3) and wa_mount_stone_putvin ('Putvin Trail / Lake of the Angels Scramble', Class 3-4) look like one climb entered twice. Both are filed under wa_mount_stone, both start at the Putvin Trailhead on FR-25, both go to Lake of the Angels, both finish by the west-ridge notch below St. Peter's Gate, and both carry identical gain_ft (5000) and dist_km (8.9) and the same aspect/face strings. The grades differ (Class 3 vs Class 3-4) and the prose differs in emphasis, so confirm before deleting either half. Variants were written for both rather than picking a winner.
_DEFECTS.mount_stone_lake_of_angels_two_coordinat: The two Mount Stone rows disagree about where Lake of the Angels is. wa_mount_stone_lake_of_angels stores it at 47.5966, -123.2736; wa_mount_stone_putvin stores it at 47.6024, -123.2611. That is roughly 1.2 km apart, and the second sits noticeably closer to the summit pin (47.6063, -123.2666) than a lake in a cirque below the south face should. A third figure, 47.602443/-123.261067, appears in the second row's own waypoint while its summit waypoint is 47.606275/-123.266425. One of these is wrong and it is the standard camp for two peaks.
_DEFECTS.lake_constance_two_coordinates: The Constance rows disagree about Lake Constance by about 2.5 km. wa_mount_constance_terrible_traverse and wa_mount_constance_finger_traverse both pin it at 47.7615, -123.108. wa_inner_constance_standard pins it at 47.750725, -123.1422 and its Lake Constance Trailhead at 47.744270, -123.142091. Independent sources put the lake near -123.14 longitude, so the -123.108 pin is the outlier and it also sits on the wrong side of the ridge for a lake at the mouth of Avalanche Canyon, which runs north from the lake toward the summit at 47.7728, -123.1273. Three routes on two peaks share this camp.
_DEFECTS.mount_skokomish_waypoints_describe_a_dif: wa_mount_skokomish_standard's approach prose says in as many words that the on-file 'Mildred Lakes / Flapjack Lakes' trailhead is wrong and that the standard route goes via the Putvin Trail and Lake of the Angels — but the WAYPOINT LIST was never updated to match. It still walks the Mildred Lakes approach step by step (Huckleberry Creek crossing, the root-ladder ridge high point at 4,100 ft, the Mildred Lakes basin between Mount Lincoln and Mount Cruiser, the off-trail brush slope above the lakes) with a Putvin trailhead pin bolted on at the end carrying a note that the existing DB trailhead 'appears to be a mismatched/incorrect entry'. The hazards array likewise still names Mildred and Flapjack. So the row currently describes two different approaches in two different columns. Both are real approaches and both are written as variants here, but the row should say which one its waypoints are for.
_DEFECTS.mount_cameron_trailhead_records_disagree: wa_mount_cameron_standard's approach_logistics names the Dosewallips Road washout (47.740259, -123.065764) as the trailhead while its approach prose calls Obstruction Point the PRIMARY approach and its entire waypoint list runs from the Obstruction Point Trailhead (47.9738, -123.4767) over Grand Pass to Cameron Basin. That is the two-copies-of-the-trailhead shape: the logistics blob and the waypoint list point at opposite sides of the range, roughly 33 km apart, and the two surfaces that read them will send a party to different roads.
_DEFECTS.mount_cameron_true_summit_disputed: The same row's summit waypoint is labelled 'Mount Cameron - East Peak (true summit)' at 7,190 ft, while its own `face` field describes a traverse 'from Cameron Pass toward the Main, Middle, and East/Southwest summits' and published traverse accounts reach the true summit FIRST from Cameron Pass and then continue to the Middle Peak and then to the East Peak. On a triple-summited peak that is a real ambiguity, and the row asserts a resolution it does not support.
_DEFECTS.mount_cameron_name_points_the_wrong_way: Recorded here as well as in the README because it is a data defect and not just a naming preference: the row is titled 'Standard Route (Southeast Slopes)' and every source describes a west-ridge walk gained at Cameron Pass, which lies west of the summit. The row's own `face` field already says 'West ridge'. Title and face contradict each other in the same row.
_DEFECTS.mount_christie_name_points_the_wrong_way: wa_mount_christie_west is titled 'West Slopes (Standard)' and its own `face` field says 'North Couloir / Christie Glacier / Southeast Ridge ... approaching via its north side', and `aspect` is N. Every published account climbs the north side. Title and face contradict each other in the same row.

_DEFECTS.mount_barnes_dist_km: wa_mount_barnes_scramble stores dist_km 85.3 (about 53 miles) against gain_ft 3200, while its approach prose describes a 26-mile round trip from Whiskey Bend with about 6,100 ft of gain, plus 6.2 miles each way added by the road washout. 85.3 km may be intended as a full Bailey Range traverse figure rather than a route distance, but paired with 3,200 ft of gain it will render as a 53-mile walk that climbs a third of a vertical kilometre.
_DEFECTS.mount_washington_summit_elevation: wa_mount_washington_olympic's routes disagree about the summit by five feet: the standard-route prose and waypoint say 6,255 ft, while wa_se_ridge_aka_shield_wall's and wa_washington_ellinor_traverse_ridge's summit waypoints say 6,260, and the area row's elevation_ft is 6260. Trivial in itself, but it is three rows on one peak.
_DEFECTS.sawtooth_ridge_and_lost_peak_absent: Two peaks named in the brief have no Olympic area in the catalog. The only 'Sawtooth' area is wa_sawtooth_chelan (Sawtooth / Lake Chelan, filed under wa_centraleast) — a different range entirely, and out of this batch's scope. The only 'Lost Peak' is wa_lost_peak_pasayten (Okanogan, 8,464 ft). The Olympic Sawtooth Ridge, in the Mount Skokomish Wilderness near Mount Cruiser, and the Olympic Lost Peak near Cameron are absent rather than misfiled — no area row for either exists under wa_olympics. Nothing was created; this is reported so a future pass does not conclude they were skipped.
